(Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Who : Phoenix Suns (7-7) @ Utah Jazz (3-13) When : 7:30 pm Arizona Time Where : Delta Center — Salt Lake City, Utah Watch : Suns+, 3TV/AZFS Listen : KMVP 98.7 Game three of this five-game road trip comes as the Suns head up to Utah. This is their first meeting with this squad this season. Unfortunately for the Jazz, injuries have derailed their season, and they’re coming off a worse record than many anticipated. For the Suns, this is no sleepwalk game, but a chance to make a key statement. A win here would give the Suns their longest win streak of the season with three, and could really be the momentum this team needs to reach its true potential. The Suns, coming off two different wins against the Denver Nuggets and Sacramento Kings, look to keep their road streak clean with zero losses. With a starting five still trying to find its footing, Jordan Ott seems to have solved the issues this lineup faced earlier in the season. The bench, though, continues to look outstanding and deserves a spot in the conversation among the best in the association. With a big game on the line, especially with it being an NBA Cup game as well, the Suns should aim to make this a statement win. Tale of the Tape Probable Starters Injury Report Suns Mark Williams — OUT (Left Shoulder Surgery) Jazz Kobe Bufkin — OUT (G League – Two-Way) Harrison Ingram — OUT (G League – Two-Way) Jaren Jackson, Jr. — OUT (Right Knee; MCL Tear) Lauri Markkanen — OUT (Right Hand Fracture) Jusuf Nurkic — OUT (R Foot; 2nd Plantar Plate Tear) What to Watch For The Suns, in their last two games, have run the same starting lineup but have staggered certain players on the bench to make it easier. That has brought some success to this team and is something to watch for in this game. Dillon Brooks has taken advantage of this switch, as it allows him to be aggressive on offense as the second unit’s lead scorer. Not only that, but it has helped on defense as well, with him more locked in. We saw this trend in the Kings game with Brooks, and with Devin Booker as well. He had a stint in the first quarter where he was left with just the bench, which let him hunt his shots and let the team take a lead to end the first. Having key guys like Jordan Goodwin, Ryan Dunn, and Collin Gillespie, who will do anything to find success and win on the court, makes it easier for guys in Brooks and Booker to be the lead offensive guys. Jordan Ott can maintain success by mixing both units, which would help the Suns find another win. Keys for a Suns Win Two things the Suns need to win against the Utah Jazz are the three-point and rebounding game. With no Jaren Jackson Jr., Jusuf Nurkic, or Lauri Markkanen, one of those should be easier than the other. The Suns cannot lose the rebounding game to Mo Bamba, who is trying to revitalize his career, or Jaxon Hayes, who has bounced from team to team. This is a weak frontcourt, and for the Suns, this is the true test for centers Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Malauch. If they are the real deal, they should excel in these matchups and prove they can handle some of the weaker frontcourts. On the three-point end, they have Keyonte George, who shoots almost 35% from three, with rookie Darryn Peterson also shooting 36%. Mix that with rotation guys like Svi Mykhailiuk and Brice Sensabough, and this Jazz team can erupt at any time from behind the arc. Key shooters Gillespie and Kennard will have to be at their best to match some of the threes this smaller Jazz team will fire off. Brooks and Booker will have to be at their best as well, since they are the two main three-point shooters in the starting five. Prediction The Suns are on the road, so handle this one like the previous one, too. Even if the Jazz court looks funky due to the NBA Cup, their team is going to look even funkier trying to score on a defense that will be bought in. Phoenix extends their longest win streak of the season while also getting their first win in Group A, taking down the Utah Jazz. Suns 123, Jazz 100

stories.title: More Than A Minor League: How The G League Builds NBA Champions
stories.summary: From 2019 Raptors legends to west coast champions, the G League has produced some of the biggest success stories of the NBA
stories.detailText: TORONTO, ON - APRIL 13: Danny Green #14 of the Toronto Raptors warms up prior to Game One of the first round of the 2019 NBA playoffs against the Orlando Magic at Scotiabank Arena on April 13, 2019 in Toronto, Canada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Vaughn Ridley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NBA G League is full of talent, littered with former collegiate stars and former lottery picks. But it’s not just a league full of flops who were never good enough for the NBA. It’s a launching point for the careers of future NBA champions and a place where struggling NBA players can find their feet and become contributors on an NBA roster once more. No G League arena knows that story better than the Mississauga Sports and Entertainment Centre. Champions and Raptors of old such as Pascal Siakam, Fred VanVleet, Norman Powell and Chris Boucher once plied their trade on the hardwood at the venue formerly known as the Hershey Centre, before a name change and a changing of the guard saw JaKobe Walter, Gradey Dick, AJ Lawson come through the doors during the era of the Paramount Fine Foods Centre in recent years. The Raptors have always been at the forefront of using the G League to find contributors and develop their own draft picks, and that should mean something to fans in Mississauga. A lot of folks in other places may scoff at the G League but it is a chapter in the stories of some of Raptors fans’ favourite players and, at the bare minimum, a footnote in the 2019 championship. While fans may know those stories, there are G League alumni littered around the NBA, many of them NBA champions who either got their start in the G or earned their way back to the NBA. The G League as a Launching Point for Champions The 2019 Raptors championship team featured two players whose stories are integral to the tale that is 2010s NBA basketball, and both of them got their start in the G and were even teammates at one point in Reno, Nevada, for the Bighorns in the 2010-11 season. Danny Green The three-time NBA champion with the Spurs, Raptors and bubble-era Lakers was drafted by Cleveland 46th overall in 2009 after an NCAA championship at UNC, but after 20 games in a rookie year in which he struggled, the Cavs cut him loose, allowing him to move on to San Antonio, where they also waived him. He landed in Nevada with the Reno Bighorns, the former G League affiliate of the Sacramento Kings. Green balled out in 16 games for Reno, leading the team in scoring with 20 points a night, as well as 7.5 rebounds per game. Arguably most importantly, he shot 43.4 per cent from deep, which was the skill that got him to the NBA and made him valuable there. He just needed a platform to show it. Jeremy Lin Jeremy Lin was Green’s teammate in Reno, albeit not for long. Lin began his NBA career in Golden State after going undrafted, a tough place to come by playing time as he sat third on the point guard depth chart behind Monta Ellis and some guy named Steph Curry. Lin spent a lot of time down in the G League with Reno, who had an affiliation with Golden State at the time. He played well and earned himself an opportunity in China during the NBA lockout before returning to North America with the Knicks the following season, and everyone knows how that went for him. San Antonio Spurs guard Danny Green tries to pull the ball away from Charlotte Hornets guard Jeremy Lin during Monday night's game at Time Warner Cable Arena on March 21, 2016 in Charlotte, N.C. The Charlotte Hornets defeated the San Antonio Spurs 91-88. (Robert Lahser/Charlotte Observer/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) That Reno Bighorns team was a launching point for Lin and Green, but it also had a roster any basketball sicko would love. Steve Novak and Hassan Whiteside suited up for the Bighorns, as did Patrick Ewing Jr, son of the Hall of Fame Knicks big man. Alex Caruso Another multi-time NBA champion, with the Lakers and Thunder, actually began his career with the Oklahoma City Blue, the G League affiliate of the OKC Thunder. His lone season with Oklahoma’s G League club led him to a Summer League invite with the Lakers and a Summer League championship alongside Lonzo Ball, Josh Hart and Kyle Kuzma. Caruso earned himself a two-way contract, which made him the first two-way signee in Lakers history. While on a two-way, he continued to play in the G League with the South Bay Lakers until his talent became so undeniable that he eventually earned himself a regular rotation spot. He’s gone on to win two championships and sign $123 million worth of NBA contracts. Reviving a Career in the G League While for Lin, Green and Caruso, the G League was where they got their first really meaningful opportunities in professional basketball, for others it has been a platform to resurrect a career that once looked dead in the water. Certain players take longer to find their role and carve out their basketball niche, and the G League can provide an opportunity away from the bright lights of the NBA. Gary Payton II Gary Payton II, son of the Hall of Fame SuperSonics legend, had actually played for the Lakers, Bucks and Wizards before finding his way to the Raptors 905 in January 2021. With the 905, Gary carved out a role for himself that should be familiar to anyone familiar with the Payton family name: defensive stopper. He won the league’s Defensive Player of the Year Award, joining Chris Boucher as the only other player to win the award as a member of the 905. Finding his role in professional basketball during his lone season with the 905 opened an opportunity for him to join the Golden State Warriors, where he won a championship in 2022 and has been an NBA player ever since. Raptors 905 centre Jamarion Sharp won the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year Award in the G League as a member of the Texas Legends. Who’s to say he can’t follow in the footsteps of Payton II and carve out a defensive role for himself in the NBA? While many fans write off the G League as a land of misfit toys and failed prospects, it is anything but that. You are highly unlikely to find future NBA All-Stars in the G League, with the exception of draft picks getting sent down for extra reps, but fans of G League teams ought to be on the lookout for the next elite-level role player like Caruso or Green, because they just might be playing in a G League gym this season.

stories.title: Fred VanVleet's 'fresh slate' is driving Houston's early season success
stories.summary: A healthy Fred VanVleet is commanding the surging Rockets after an ACL injury derailed his 2025-26 season. Here's why he's so important.
stories.detailText: FRED VANVLEET BOILED inside watching the Houston Rockets "floating," he'd later say, as the Utah Jazz transformed a 12-point deficit into a 10-point lead over a span of 7 minutes, 39 seconds of a game he knew "was there for the taking." "He was pissed off," Rockets coach Ime Udoka said, "and kind of went off on everybody." VanVleet also unleashed that fury on the Jazz, who eventually fell 125-118 on Nov. 13 in an NBA Cup matchup, as VanVleet racked up 10 of his 17 points in the third quarter, catalyzing a 15-2 Rockets run heading into the final period. Alperen Sengun jokingly revealed a new nickname for the point guard after the game: "Admiral." VanVleet, 32, is navigating his NBA career now with more purpose, after acknowledging he had taken it for granted. It's a realization VanVleet came to while sitting out a 2025-26 campaign that teemed with expectations after Kevin Durant 's arrival. The point guard sustained a torn ACL at a workout in the Bahamas before training camp, leaving the Rockets without a veteran floor leader and bound for a second straight first-round postseason exit . But the undersized, self-made veteran is steering the ship again in Houston. VanVleet is transforming the Rockets into contenders in the Western Conference, sitting at 12-4 and one game out of the 1-seed. The Rockets rank 10th in assist-to-turnover ratio and 14th in turnover percentage after finishing 27th in both categories last season. VanVleet ranks fifth in the NBA in assist-to-turnover ratio (5.07) among players logging at least 25 minutes per game. He has also improved Houston's spacing, having taken 66% of his shots from 3-point range, good for ninth among players to attempt 100 shots or more. He's also knocking down those long balls, connecting on 39.8% from range, which would register as the second-best 3-point percentage of his career. Most of all, VanVleet provides the calming steady hand that Houston missed in his absence last season. The Rockets finished 22-23 last season in clutch time -- defined by any game separated by five points or fewer in the final five minutes of the fourth quarter or overtime -- with VanVleet watching from the bench. "We obviously missed his end-of-game stuff last season, but just his calming presence on the court, getting guys set in their spots [is what VanVleet provides]," Udoka told ESPN. "He always takes what the game gives him. So, he's picking the spots as far as scoring and getting guys involved. Some of our endgame situations last year were due to a lack of I would say poise at the end from a veteran leader." VANVLEET POINTS OUT he was having "one of my best summers" when word came down the Rockets were trading for Durant in June. For VanVleet, adding Durant "symbolized at that moment that, 'OK, we're competing for a championship this year.' And that was the part that was like, 'All right, boom, I've got to get my mind ready and get right to compete for a chip.'" VanVleet had already taken care of the physical part of preparation. Then in late July, he boarded a near 12-hour flight to Istanbul, where he spent a week working with Sengun to optimize pick-and-roll actions and angles on screens. VanVleet and Sengun also participated in 3-on-3 and 5-on-5 runs against members of the Turkish national team. By the time the Rockets convened in the Bahamas ahead of training camp, the first day the entire team was together in the gym, VanVleet wanted to impart some wisdom on playing alongside a generational superstar. VanVleet was part of the 2019 Toronto Raptors squad that defeated Durant's Golden State Warriors in six games after a midseason trade with the San Antonio Spurs sent Kawhi Leonard to Toronto. "I was letting everybody know because I went through it with Kawhi [Leonard]," VanVleet said. "Nothing changes just because we added KD. We've still got to be us." Naturally, VanVleet would demonstrate on the court in an open gym run with his teammates. "So, I'm having a day," he said. "I'm balling." Then, just as quickly, something in his right leg popped. "You could feel the air come out of the gym," VanVleet said. "Then, we did little tests and s--- like that. I didn't think it was that bad. I thought maybe I'd be out a couple weeks, maybe miss the preseason. "But ultimately, when we got the MRI, that's when it was real." VanVleet underwent ACL surgery that September and vowed to return to the team later that season, not because he believed he'd recover quickly to join them on the court, "but just to keep the guys locked in," he explained. "Just because I went down don't mean to give up the f---ing season." VanVleet wouldn't let them, anyway. A couple of weeks after the surgery, his phone started to buzz with texts from teammates that he acknowledges kept him focused throughout the rehab process. "Yo, we need you around," one text read. Another said: "We just need you here. We need your voice." VanVleet couldn't walk for five weeks after the surgery and said he had to learn to run and jump again. "I'm appreciative now of every second of what it means to be in the NBA," he said. "You can lose sight of that. It's just natural as a human. We just take advantage. You take for granted your health until you wake up and you've got the flu. Everybody walking around is taking for granted walking." VanVleet would spend all of last season at most of the team's meetings, practices and games -- both home and away -- working with some of younger players such as Amen Thompson and Reed Sheppard on pick-and-roll reads as the Rockets tried to replace their veteran point guard with inexperienced ball handlers. Thompson had spent his first two seasons locked mainly into the dunker spot, and the coaching staff pushed him into learning a totally new position so he could serve as VanVleet's primary replacement. Sheppard was coming off a rookie season in which he started only three games and played primarily off the ball. Durant, Sengun, Jabari Smith Jr . and Tari Eason would all take turns throughout the season initiating the offense. But none of them could match VanVleet's reliability, especially late in games. Game 3 of Houston's opening-round loss to the Los Angeles Lakers showed just how much. With Durant out because of a sore left ankle, the Rockets led by six points with 30 seconds remaining, on the verge of winning their first game of the series. Then things went haywire for an inexperienced squad missing their floor leader. First, Houston fouled on a 3-point attempt with 25 seconds left in regulation after a turnover, and the Lakers knocked down all three free throws to pull to within three points. Then, LeBron James picked Sheppard clean for a steal and hit a 3-pointer to tie the score at 101 with 13 seconds left. Those "horrendous mistakes," as Udoka described them that night , caused Houston to fall 112-108 in overtime . The Rockets eventually lost the series 4-2. "He would tell me [during that time] to just take it a day at a time," Thompson told ESPN about VanVleet. "It was a new thing. Going from playing damn near power forward to point guard, it's different. He knows there's a lot that comes with that. That first year for point guards is hard. So, he was always keeping me locked in. He was genuinely great." Still, all the time spent off the floor playing pseudo-coach changed how VanVleet viewed his career. "Because of my story and where I come from, I always felt like I had good perspective," VanVleet said. "I felt like I was always very appreciative of the moment and grateful. But you don't really have a real understanding of that until it's taken away from you. So, to not be able to play, to not be active, to sit out a full year, it gives you an appreciation for the small s---. I've had a hell of a career so far and now it's like, 'OK, you get another chance to have a fresh slate.'" ON A COOL , damp Tuesday at Memorial Hermann, the Rockets' training center, Udoka cracked a smile, pondering the notion of VanVleet's ability to hold his coaching staff just as accountable as his teammates. "He's the most vocal," Udoka said. "He's got the IQ, experience, all those things. We can move him all around. For instance, put him on guards one night. Put him on Draymond Green another night, different things like that, and he recognizes everything. He has a really good feel for what to get us into to get guys shots and a feel for who needs to get involved, who to keep hot." Udoka says he considers VanVleet an extension of the coaching staff, holding everyone accountable. VanVleet's return has eased the ballhandling burden of both Thompson and Durant, which has played a role in reducing turnovers. Durant finished last season with the 10th-most turnovers (3.2 per game) in the NBA, and now his touches per game (50.3) are his fewest in a season since player tracking began in 2013. Durant's 3.1-second average touch length ranks as his lowest in a season since 2016-17 after finishing 2025-26 with the highest touch length (3.8 seconds) of his career. Thompson, meanwhile, has brought the ball up the court this season for an average of 20.2 possessions, down from 31.4 last season, and his average touch length has fallen from 3.8 seconds last season to 3.1. "It's just control," Smith said. "It's ball security, just knowing what we're going to get to when he's on the floor. The main thing late in the games is getting up shots and not turning the ball over. He adds that ball security and knows how to slow down the game, knowing what we're going to get to, what set we're going to run and what matchup we like." The Rockets have faced four of the top eight teams in the West, winning three of those matchups, including victories over the Spurs, Denver Nuggets and Oklahoma City Thunder . Though Houston's 3-3 record in clutch time isn't much better than last season's mark (22-23), the team has cut turnovers in clutch time in half from 1.6 to 0.8 -- a direct result of VanVleet's steady hand in crucial moments. The veteran has dished 71 assists with 14 turnovers so far. VanVleet will become an unrestricted free agent at the end of the season. But he isn't approaching what could be his final season in Houston with a chip on his shoulder. Throughout the early portion of the schedule, he has sat out of the second night of back-to-backs but hopes to ramp up his workload to play every night as the season progresses. "I believe in betting on yourself, but I never really played for myself," VanVleet said. "I believe the better the team does, it's a reflection on me. I made a s--- ton of money based on being good to the game, being a good teammate and playing the right way. So, I'm not going to change that now." VanVleet demonstrated as much with his third-quarter tongue-lashing on the Rockets' bench against the Jazz on Nov. 13, the same night Sengun became the third player in Rockets history to tally 40 points, 10 rebounds and five assists on 70% shooting, joining the company of Yao Ming (2004) and Hakeem Olajuwon (1994). VanVleet has thrived with on-ball screens this season, ranking seventh in points per direct pick among ball handlers to run 100-plus plays. He also has been an extremely effective partner working with Sengun in inverted pick-and-rolls. "He comes out there, wakes everybody up, plays his ass off and helps everybody," Sengun said. ESPN Research contributed to this story.

stories.title: Sources: Brandon Ingram (Achilles) expected to Clippers debut vs. Rockets
stories.summary: After recovering from Achilles surgery, Brandon Ingram is set to make his Clippers debut Monday against the Rockets, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.
stories.detailText: LA Clippers two-time All-Star Brandon Ingram is expected to make his season and team debut on Monday against the Houston Rockets , sources tell ESPN. Ingram returns to action after undergoing surgery for a partially torn Achilles tendon in May. The Clippers acquired Ingram in the long-delayed trade that sent Kawhi Leonard back to the Toronto Raptors . Shortly before the start of the season, the Clippers made the surprise announcement that Ingram was recovering from the Achilles tear. Ingram had missed the final two games of Toronto's first-round loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers last April. He had surgery in May and, during the procedure, doctors discovered and repaired a partially torn Achilles. The Clippers were aware of the injury and elongated rehab timeline when they opted to execute the trade. Ingram, 29, averaged 21.5 points, 5.6 rebounds and 3.7 assists last season for the Raptors and will enter the lineup for a Clippers team that enters Friday with a 4-10 record. Information from ESPN's Ben Golliver and Anthony Slater was used in this report.

stories.title: ANALYSIS: Day’Ron Sharpe is emerging as a bright spot despite the Nets’ ugly start
stories.summary: Vibes might be low in NetsWorld, but at least Day’Ron Sharpe is proving his worth.
stories.detailText: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 18: Day'ron Sharpe #20 of the Brooklyn Nets looks on during the first quarter against the Chicago Bulls at Barclays Center on November 18, 2026 in New York City. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images Things aren’t pretty in Brooklyn right now, not even close. The Nets are 3-11, and even though the record looks bad, the way they keep losing adds to the frustration. Brooklyn is coming off an embarrassing 137-107 loss to a Chicago Bulls team that entered the game with just two wins. Beyond that, the team has now lost five games by at least 15 points this season, the most in the NBA. It doesn’t stop there, either. The Nets have allowed 135+ points in back-to-back games for the first time since April 1969! So, yeah, optimism is pretty hard to come by these days. That’s to put it mildly, of course. But for the fearless, ride-or-die fans out there anxiously searching for something, just anything, to feel good about, there is a bright spot worth discussing. That bright spot goes by the name Day’Ron Sharpe. Sharpe, 25, is the longest-tenured player currently on Brooklyn’s roster, in his sixth season with the organization. After the team dealt Nic Claxton to Chicago over the summer in a three-team deal with the Minnesota Timberwolves to bring in Julius Randle, this is Sharpe’s first year as the Nets’ full-time starting center. Throughout his career, analytics have always loved Sharpe, particularly for his offensive rebounding. Entering this season, though, the question was more about whether that efficiency would translate to a larger sample size. And so far, it has continued, and then some. According to Cleaning the Glass , the Nets have been 18.4 points per 100 possessions better with Sharpe on the floor than without him, placing him in the 93rd percentile among all forwards and bigs who have played a minute this season. While rebounding has always been his big calling card, the biggest difference in Sharpe’s on/off numbers seems to come on offense. The Nets have scored 13.0 more points per 100 possessions with the North Carolina product on the court, which ranks in the 95th percentile. It’s also the seventh-biggest discrepancy among forwards and bigs. For perspective, his overall on/off differential currently ranks ahead of notable names like Nikola Jokić (+15.5) and Alperen Şengün (+15.5). He’s also just one percentile beyond Karl-Anthony Towns. All three of those players are averaging over 30 minutes per game, compared to Sharpe’s 23.6, but that certainly doesn’t make it something to scoff at. Sharpe is no stranger to ranking high in efficiency categories, but the most encouraging part is that he’s doing it with an expanded workload so far. Through 14 games, he is averaging over 23 minutes per night. His career high in a single season before this was last year, when he averaged 18.7 in 62 games. So, the big man has never averaged over 20 minutes per night before this season. He’s also started all 14 games for Brooklyn this year, already shattering his previous career-high in starts per season, which was just eight in his rookie campaign. Day'Ron Sharpe has a +16.7 net rating swing for the Nets. That's the 4th-highest in the NBA among qualified centers. Sharpe over his last 6 games: 9.5 points 7.0 rebounds 6.5 assists 2.2 turnovers (3.0 ast/to) 1.7 blocks 19/34 FG (56%) 16/19 FT (84%) 3/8 3P Playing good ball. pic.twitter.com/3CvRZwszua — Erik Slater (@ErikSlater_) November 13, 2026 Overall, Sharpe, who re-signed on a two-year, $20 million contract this offseason, has averaged 8.4 points, 7.1 rebounds (including 3.3 offensive boards), and 4.0 assists on 52.9% shooting. Another encouraging number is the 4.0 assists per game. With Claxton out of the picture, Sharpe has taken on a much bigger role as the offensive facilitator. He’s done a really solid job of embracing the responsibility that comes with being an offensive hub. It’s a role Claxton anchored for years in Brooklyn. That’s especially important for a Nets team that still seems to be searching for an identity and consistency on offense. The passing isn’t necessarily new, either. Sharpe had flashed that in smaller doses throughout his career. Now that he is getting the opportunites, it’s becoming even more obvious. Against the Atlanta Hawks on November 7, he dropped 13 assists and his first career triple-double. The 13 assists were the most in a single game by a Nets center in franchise history. Day'Ron Sharpe vs. Hawks · 12 PTS, 13 AST, 10 REB · First career triple-double · Most assists in a single game by a Nets center in franchise history pic.twitter.com/2v63bh6MT1 — Brooklyn Nets (@BrooklynNets) November 8, 2026 For me, the biggest concern regarding Brooklyn’s squad entering the year was their lack of rim protection after dealing Claxton. That left a big void, and the Nets didn’t do much over the summer to fix it. They added Mo Wagner, but as fans have seen, he is much more of an offensive player and that’s being kind. That’s not to downplay his impact; his offensive ability is certainly important, but he has limitations down low. It’s never been a strength of Sharpe’s either. As a result, the team is currently allowing 48.7 paint points per game, the ninth-most in the NBA. For a team like Brooklyn that lacks elite-level firepower and just plain athleticism, it’s difficult to win consistently when you’re allowing nearly 50 points per game in the paint. By no means does all of that responsibility fall on Sharpe, though. Sean Marks deserves criticism for structuring the roster that way, and his frontcourt teammates also haven’t necessarily helped turn the tide in that facet. Ultimately, his start to the year has been very promising. Digging deeper than the sheer numbers, the continued efficiency and success while playing at a career-high rate is exactly why fans should be excited moving forward. There are still 68 games to play, but so far, Sharpe is making the most of his extended role.

stories.title: Ranking all the scary comments Steph Curry makes in the ESPN article
stories.summary: Stephen Curry’s in pain and that’s got him thinking about the end of his playing days. We’re not ready.
stories.detailText: SAN FRANCISCO, CA - NOVEMBER 7: Stephen Curry #30 of the Golden State Warriors run off to the court after the game against the Orlando Magic on November 7, 2026 at Chase Center in San Francisco, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Jed Jacobsohn/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Three days ago, ESPN’s Anthony Slater published a story that served to remind us all that time slows for no one and that Steph Curry’s playing days are numbered. It was startling. The specifics of it were so definitive, so obviously instructive of how the music would suddenly stop, that many fans were (rightfully) shook. Every quote feels like a night night dagger; but, since this is a sports blog, let’s rank them by order of “ BANG! ”-itude. First: if you haven’t read the piece, go and read it, because I’ll be jumping around. 8. “I assumed that it would probably be one of, if not the last, contract I signed. I’m not afraid to say it. But maybe I’ll surprise myself and want to keep going.” Is this actually a scary quote? Not totally. We must always remember that a professional athlete who has played at the highest level possible for a human being during this moment in time lives in the moment most of the time. But you know the end is on the horizon once the athlete begins to discuss the end. Most of our stars have been stuck in some version of that kid who loved the game they played and wound up making millions for doing and mere recognition of mortality is revolutionary in terms of self-reflection. But the scare factor is that Steph’s aware the party’s winding down. His body has been telling him, and now his conscious thought has joined the fray. 7. “I know how blessed I am to even still have the ability to convince myself that I could be the best player on a championship-contending team,” Curry said. This is a heightening of that recognition. A recognition of context, but also “the ability to convince myself” is a heckuva self-reflection. His mind is asking his body to prove it, and — for now — it’s satisfying his standards. Will he lower his standards to keep convincing himself? Or does he have a “If I can’t do ‘x’ anymore, then that’s it” in mind? 6. “Throttle the general intensity back […] I should feel like I left a little bit on the table as opposed to just exhausting [everything].” Slater gets quotes from Steve Kerr in this piece, too, and for this segment he relates: “He’s staying off his feet [more often],” Kerr said. “Relying on the fact that he’s built up this incredible skill level that’s not going to leave him. Then, he’s found a way to stay really fit without pounding the knees, the ankles. He’s on the bike, underwater treadmill. He’s creative.” But I’m putting this 8th because I’m a little scared by how this aging curve seems to have surprised Curry. Slater begins the article by talking about earlier this year, and that being the first time he really seemed to have grappled with his aging body. Every athlete — every human being! — is different, of course, so this isn’t a criticism, it’s just a note that Steph Curry is not one of those athletes who plans too far ahead. His greatness has been defined by putting the pedal to the metal at all times; but, everyone in their mid-thirties would be wise to reassess their body maintenance. You can see how the idea of leaving something on the table doesn’t appeal to him. It’s not a lack of wisdom or intelligence, it’s just the way that he is wired. But as a fan reading this, the fear factor is in how he’s just going to keep dancing until the music stops. 5. “I want to appreciate what’s happening right now because I don’t want to just go through the motions. Then, it passes you by.” Well, okay, and then there’s an acknowledgement that he needs to slow some aspect of it down. This line definitely amps up the bummer vibes of the piece. It’s like he’s counting how many sunrises he’s got left. 4. “It sucks because it’s a part of your mortality,” Curry said of the constant aging reminders. “Basketball mortality.” Or counting how many more sandwiches he’ll have left to eat in his life. But you can see why Dylan Thomas urged rage because contemplation or otherwise quiet reflection is just a bummer. It sucks to be reminded that this is all going to end — better to burn out than fade away, right? But that’s the tension of being a professional athlete. That’s certainly the trajectory Steph is on; will this slowdown prolong his career? 3. “That was the moment where I started to get concerned,” Curry said. “It just didn’t feel right.” This is the first quote of the aptly titled article, “The clock is ticking on Steph Curry’s final act with the Warriors.” Slater starts with an anecdote about an off-day workout going awry and quickly pulls in the oblique abdominal strain, but the constant throughout the article is Steph’s knee. “barking” “a weird soreness and pain that didn’t go away” “deteriorated” “It was basically holding. It wasn’t going either direction.” There’s even discussion of how much it held him back, where he was just going through the motions while on the court at times. This is as close to a medical assessment as we get in the piece, and it’s devastating. Cartilage doesn’t come back as we age thanks to how blood flow works in the area. That’s where things like stem cell therapy come into play. But, at this point, it’s pretty clear that after all the miles Steph Curry has logged over the years, we’re talking about patching an engine that’s getting near the end of its life. Consider this part one of a two-part idea. Part two: 2. “You look at the calendar. Then, you start thinking about more of the existential part of it. Will I have to deal with this the rest of my career? Is it something that will … what’s the word … will it diminish what I’m able to do on the court?” As terrible a setback as the oblique abdominal strain/tear is, this quote plus the one before it really does point to his knee being the ticking time bomb, and that he’s well aware that’s the case. 1. “I tried to go harder, and there were certain directions of movement and stuff that just didn’t work. That was the true setback,” Curry said while shaking his head. “I couldn’t even get to the point where I could play. Even just getting spot shots, it felt worse than it had before.” The story is that Stephen Curry had the biggest setback of his professional career this calendar year and because his body has started to break down. It doesn’t get any scarier than that. This year is almost over. What horror(s) will next year bring? But I’ll end this post … the least scary thing Curry says in the whole piece. If circumstances demanded it, Curry said he would’ve been fine sliding into more of a complementary role late in his career, similar to most fading stars. Perhaps he eventually will. “It would not kill my ego,” Curry said. “I want to win. Whatever that means, you make decisions based on what’s in front of you.” You’re not going to find any Stephen Curry followers who don’t think the guy has a degree of humility about him. That’s part of what makes him special. He might be the greatest. At times, even he might even acknowledge that he’s “up there,” in terms of the all-time greats. But he’s also aware of how fleeting that feeling can be. It won’t be long before he’s an afterthought. He’s certainly been in the league long enough to see opinions, rankings, or simply stature diminish or outright disappear overnight. And there’s also the thing where, sometimes, we need to say something out loud just to convince ourselves it’s true. We don’t know when Curry will return from his current injury, but there’s still just a bit more time left for us to enjoy a bit more history created by his play. If this isn’t the last ride, then it’s the penultimate one.

stories.title: NBA trade rumors 2026-27: Dejounte Murray update (or, non-update), Kyrie Irving, Trey Murphy, more
stories.summary: Don't expect any deals until after a lot of summer contracts become trade-eligible on Dec. 15.
stories.detailText: Don't expect any NBA trades before Dec. 15, when many of the players who signed new contracts or extensions this summer become eligible to be traded. Even then, it's more likely we'll get closer to the February trade deadline before we see any notable names moved. That includes the guy in the sub-headline below. No traction in Dejounte Murray trade While the insatiable NBA rumor mill keeps trying to find clickable updates on Dejounte Murray trades — "The Pelicans talked to the Suns!!!" — the reality is there is no traction toward any kind of deal for the New Orleans guard. Grant Liffman and Chris Mannix break it down well in the video above, but here is the latest. • Murray, through his agents at Klutch Sports, made a trade request, and the Pelicans publicly acknowledged that, saying, "We will evaluate potential trade opportunities that are in the best interest of our organization." New Orleans hasn't found that yet. Meanwhile, Murray's body language on the court betrays how unhappy he is, and he is shooting 29.6% from 3-point range this season, which doesn't help his trade value. • To be blunt, teams around the league view Murray as a negative value contract. Those are hard to trade. The fact he is making $32.8 million this season and has a $30.8 million player option for next season also gives teams pause. He is viewed as a 30-year-old guard who's shot 41.9% overall and 30% from 3 in the last two-plus seasons. • While Murray's camp seems to continue to push the Suns as a destination, league sources have told NBC Sports the Suns have minimal interest, unless the Pelicans want to attach sweetener, such as a first-round pick. That’s been reported a lot of other places as well , it's no secret. While the Suns could use a point guard and have done background work on Murray (according to Brian Windhorst of ESPN), they aren't sold on Murray being the All-Star player he was five years ago, and he hasn't looked the same coming off his torn Achilles. How much interest the Pelicans have in Jalen Green should be another question. • When teams do call the Pelicans, they are more likely to ask about Trey Murphy III and Herb Jones. But Joe Dumars is keeping the price ridiculously high — the Pelicans turned down a trade that would have netted them at least two first-round picks for Murphy over the summer, Michael Scotto of Hoopshype reports . • Jake Fischer of The Stein Line reports the Suns are more interested in adding a big man with Mark Williams out for the season. Other trade rumors • Utah is one of the teams giving "internal consideration" a potential Kyrie Irving trade, if (or, more likely when) the Mavericks start listening to offers, r eports Ian Begley of SNY.TV . It's worth noting that teams have internal discussions about a lot of players and deals that they never even bother to reach out to the other team about in a serious manner, and where Irving fits in the young timeline in Utah is a good question, but the rumor is out there. • Multiple reports have coach Brian Keefe's seat in Washington getting hot. This was a team that made moves for veterans in Anthony Davis (playing well) and Trae Young (not playing well) to try and win now, and with the team off to a 5-11 start, someone may be the scapegoat. Washington should have just pivoted to building around AJ Dybantsa, but they are going to be stuck with that horrible four-year, $212 million extension they gave Young this summer for a while. That is the most untradable contract in the league right now. • Multiple reports have teams interested in trading for Bulls guard Tre Jones. Here is what Zach Lowe said on his Ringer podcast: "Teams are already calling the Bulls about Tre Jones... if he's not the best backup point guard in the NBA, he's very close. If they trade him, they're gonna get real stuff."

Quarterfinals Dec. 8 and/or Dec. 9: Semifinals Dec. 11: Championship NBA Cup FAQ: Everything to know What is the format? NBA commissioner Adam Silver has had a longstanding fascination with European soccer. Establishing an in-season cup competition within the NBA schedule came from soccer leagues having both a regular-season title, won by the team with the most points over the full year, and a separate tournament (or, in some leagues, multiple tournaments) that runs concurrently with the league season. In England, for example, there are the various divisions -- led by the Premier League -- and also the FA Cup competition. But unlike those European leagues, which play their cup competitions outside of their league schedules, the NBA Cup is built in to the regular-season slate. The 30 NBA teams are split into six five-team groups -- three featuring Eastern Conference teams and three comprising Western Conference teams -- with each team then playing one game against the other four in its group. The winner of each group, plus the team with the best record among the non-group winners, advances to the knockout stage of the competition. How will this impact the regular-season schedule and standings? Typically, the NBA sends out a full 82-game schedule in mid-August. Now, the league sends out only 80 games and leaves a gap of roughly a week to fill in later, depending on how the group stage of the NBA Cup plays out. The two teams from the East and West that lose in the quarterfinals will play their 82nd game against each other. Meanwhile, the 22 teams that fail to qualify for the knockout rounds will have their final two games scheduled -- one at home and one on the road against others eliminated in the group stage. The teams that reach the NBA Cup final will actually play 83 games -- though the championship game won't count toward the standings or any statistical markers. The four teams that reach the semifinals will have completed their 82 games and won't need any other games added to their schedule. Any team that makes it to the semifinals will have that game moved later in the schedule to avoid back-to-back games. The NBA made this change in an effort to avoid having empty days on the calendar while attempting to minimize back-to-backs for all teams as much as possible. Where are the semifinals and final being played? In a shift from previous tournaments, the quarterfinals and semifinals will be played at home sites. The Dec. 11 title game, meanwhile, will move from Las Vegas to the storied Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis. NBA commissioner Adam Silver previously said the league was searching for "storied college arenas" to play host to the Cup final. (No venue has been announced for 2027.) Why does the NBA Cup include regular-season games? Before its launch, one of the main questions surrounding the in-season tournament was why any team would be incentivized to compete in it. The NBA ensured teams will be motivated by making every game part of the season and, as in-conference matchups, potentially important to playoff tiebreakers. If this had been set up like the cup tournaments in European soccer, there would have been nothing stopping NBA teams from opting out by sitting their top players for extra rest. Which teams make up the groups? To create the groups, the NBA put the 15 teams in each conference into five pots, separated by their finish last season. Pot 1 included the teams that finished in the top three in the regular-season standings, Nos. 4-6 in the standings went into Pot 2, Nos. 7-9 into Pot 3, Nos. 10-12 into Pot 4 and Nos. 13-15 into Pot 5. As a result, the following groups were drawn: East Group A Detroit Pistons Toronto Raptors Orlando Magic Milwaukee Bucks Brooklyn Nets East Group B New York Knicks Cleveland Cavaliers Philadelphia 76ers Miami Heat Indiana Pacers East Group C Boston Celtics Atlanta Hawks Charlotte Hornets Chicago Bulls Washington Wizards West Group A Denver Nuggets Houston Rockets Phoenix Suns Dallas Mavericks Utah Jazz West Group B Oklahoma City Thunder Minnesota Timberwolves LA Clippers New Orleans Pelicans Memphis Grizzlies West Group C San Antonio Spurs Los Angeles Lakers Portland Trail Blazers Golden State Warriors Sacramento Kings Does one group stand out the most from the others? East Group B is a monster. All five teams -- defending NBA Cup and Finals champion New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Miami and Indiana -- are among the favorites to win the conference in 2026-27. The group stage will also feature reunion games for LeBron James , when the 76ers face the Cavs and Heat. And after guard Tyrese Haliburton missed the entire 2025-26 season while rehabbing a torn Achilles, the Pacers will be back among the East elite and hungry to reach the title game in Indianapolis. What do players get for winning? In 2023, the first year the tournament was held, the players on the winning team received $500,000 each and the runners-up got $200,000. The losing players of the semifinals each got $100,000, and those ousted in the quarterfinals got $50,000. Now, in each subsequent year, the prizes will be slightly higher, as a result of negotiated raises year over year to keep pace with increases in the salary cap and basketball-related income as part of the most recent collective bargaining agreement between the NBA and the National Basketball Players Association. Will anyone earn individual honors for their play in NBA Cup games? There will be an MVP award, as well as an all-tournament team. Will this have any impact on the playoffs? Not beyond the games counting in the regular-season standings (and toward tiebreakers). The only playoff impact comes from the wins and losses accrued throughout the tournament. Though there was debate among league insiders about guaranteeing a playoff berth for winning the tournament, ultimately that idea (or any other to further incentivize teams) was not enacted. Why is it called the Emirates NBA Cup? The league struck a sponsorship deal with Emirates, the Dubai-based airline, to sponsor the tournament after its initial run. The NBA said last year that it went with the most basic titles for both the tournament and its trophy -- the "in-season tournament" and "NBA Cup" -- as a way to introduce the concept to fans. However, using such nondescript names had another clear advantage: It gave the league a blank slate in case it sold the naming rights for the tournament and cup to a sponsor and avoided the complications that could arise by naming them after someone (for example, late NBA commissioner David Stern, one possibility that had been floated before the tournament was officially unveiled). stories.title: Braelon Allen making case for more touches in Jets’ crowded backfield
stories.summary: Jets RB Braelon Allen has rushed for 638 yards this season, but head coach Aaron Glenn says starter Breece Hall remains the team's top option.
stories.detailText: Braelon Allen averaged less than six carries per game as a rookie. Last season, the Jets’ backup running back was limited to only four games due to a knee injury . Take flight with the Jets Text with Brian Costello all season as he brings Sports+ subscribers the latest Jets intel from on the field and off. tRY IT NOW But the 134th player — and 11th running back — selected in the 2024 draft was ready when opportunity arrived. While Breece Hall was sidelined by a quad injury , Allen ran for 504 yards (5.4 yards per carry) in his first five career starts, opening this month with a 147-yard effort that made him the first Jets running back in 11 years (Chris Ivory) to rush for 100 yards in consecutive games. Entering Week 11, the 22-year-old is one of only eight running backs in the NFL averaging at least five yards per carry. New York Jets running back Braelon Allen (0) looks on before a game against the Buffalo Bills in East Rutherford, New Jersey, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect “I know what I can be in this league,” Allen told The Post on Friday. “You needed the platform to show what you’re capable of. I always knew when that time came I was gonna take advantage. “Fortunately, but unfortunately, I came to a place where they had a really good running back already.” Once again, touches have become hard to find for one of the Jets’ most dynamic players. In returning to a backup role over the past two games, Allen has rushed for 73 yards on 16 carries (three receptions, 27 yards), while Hall had 26 rushes for 102 rushing yards (seven receptions, 93 yards). This season, Hall has 265 rushing yards (3.4 yards per carry) and one touchdown in five games, while Allen has 638 rushing yards and three touchdowns in 10 games. Still, head coach Aaron Glenn reiterated Friday that Hall — who signed a three-year, $43.5 million deal in the offseason — remains the team’s top option in the backfield. New York Jets running back Breece Hall (20) runs past Cleveland Browns linebacker Carson Schwesinger (49) in East Rutherford, N.J., Nov. 9, 2025. USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect “Obviously, Breece and Garrett [Wilson] are guys that we really try to target for the most part, and then we make sure the rest of the guys get their touches when they come,” Glenn said. “I think, obviously, Breece will end up getting a tick more [touches] because, again, he’s our starting running back, but we want to make sure that Braelon gets his touches.” There has been a greater effort made to include the backup in the past two weeks than there was in the Jets’ first three games, when Hall received 51 carries and Allen got 19. But there is no clear solution to finding the right balance. “We should talk about it because that’s what people want to know,” offensive coordinator Frank Reich said this week. “I think that’s a great problem to have. For me, it’s terrible because I can’t win. I know it’s never gonna be enough. I’m not worried about that to the outside. I’m worried about that when I walk in the room with the guys. “I’m not worried about the fantasy stuff and all that stuff. I’m worried about those guys in the locker room and I want them to know — and I know they do — how much I believe in each one of them and how much I want to give each one of them the ball, but there’s only so many touches in a game. “They have a lot of respect for each other. I wish we could get it to them both more, but that’s just the way it’s gonna be.”

stories.title: Cardinals QB Carson Beck dealing with back spasms; Josh Johnson may start
stories.summary: The Cardinals are preparing veteran quarterback Josh Johnson to start Sunday vs. the Chiefs as rookie Carson Beck deals with back spasms, coach Mike LaFleur said Friday.
stories.detailText: TEMPE, Ariz. -- The Cardinals are preparing veteran quarterback Josh Johnson to start Sunday in Kansas City as rookie Carson Beck deals with back spasms, coach Mike LaFleur said Friday. Beck is dealing with the same back issue that's been lingering all season and it "just kind of flared up," LaFleur said. Beck will not practice Friday, the second straight day he will have missed practice. However, LaFleur isn't closing the door on the possibility of Beck playing. "Just taking it one minute at a time right now, not even one day at a time, taking one minute," LaFleur said. "It's basically just kind of responding to the treatment, see how he feels when he wakes up tomorrow." LaFleur doesn't think Beck's injury will keep him out multiple weeks but said, "I can't go there yet." Beck has been preparing like he typically does, LaFleur said, in the event he's able to play. LaFleur expressed some unhappiness with not being able to see Beck continue as Arizona's starter for a second straight week. "I'd be lying to you if I said that would be OK not seeing him go on Sunday, but it is what it is," LaFleur said. "Show goes on this league. I mean, this ball's getting put down at noon on Sunday and we're going to go." With Arizona on its fourth quarterback of the season, LaFleur said the Cardinals are back to square one with the offense. "There's no next step of the playbook," LaFleur said. "This is going back to the starting, the table of contents right now. And that's OK. That's OK. For a three-and-a-half hour window, it's my job to figure out whatever we can to get the ball moving forward." Should Beck not be able to play Sunday and Johnson gets the start, rookie quarterback Joey Aguilar will be the backup and wide receiver Devin Duvernay will be the emergency third quarterback, LaFleur said. He added that Arizona prepared Duvernay to be the emergency quarterback a couple weeks ago. LaFleur worked with Johnson in 2020 in San Francisco when LaFleur was the 49ers' receivers coach and in 2021 with the Jets as their offensive coordinator. The two have stayed in touch since, LaFleur said. "The cool part is if it is Josh, I've called plays for him before and had a really great experience calling plays for him," LaFleur said. LaFleur added: "He knows me, I know him, he's done it all. So, we'll have those conversations if he ends up being the guy through today, through tomorrow, all the way up into Sunday about, 'Hey, what do we like? What we not?' No different than we would with any of the quarterbacks." The 40-year-old Johnson is now on his 15th NFL team. LaFleur said his talent and his ability to be a good teammate has kept him around since getting drafted in 2008. "He is incredible in the quarterback room," LaFleur said. "He's incredible for the starter. He's incredible for young quarterbacks. In terms of just the way he sees the game, his energy, his positivity, how he keeps it real, he's mature and he can still sling it." LaFleur said Aguilar has been experiencing "a little welcome to the NFL moment here" with the quarterback carousel Arizona is on. Beck became Arizona's starter last week after Gardner Minshew II was lost for the season with a right UCL injury. Minshew took over the starting role for the Cardinals after they traded Jacoby Brissett in Week 9. Both Johnson and Aguilar were signed by the Cardinals on Nov. 10. Beck and Aguilar are both 25 years old, prompting LaFleur to quip that he believes Arizona has the two oldest rookie quarterbacks in the league at the moment. And pairing them with a 40-year-old veteran led to LaFleur doing some funny math. With the "median age with Josh, man, I think these guys have been in the league for quite some time," LaFleur said with a smile.

stories.title: At 7-2, Have the Bears Met or Exceeded Your Preseason Expectations?
stories.summary: A few of the WCG crew looks back on their preseason record prediction for the Bears.
stories.detailText: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Head Coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears walks out to the field prior to the game against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears have completed what Ben Johnson would refer to as “2 quarters” of the 2026 NFL season. Despite early adversity, they’ve managed to come away with only two losses so far – a mark that would be more impressive if they weren’t still sitting in 3rd place in their division. Still, the halfway point of the season presents us with a great opportunity to look back at the record predictions of a few of our WCG writers and evaluate just how close we each were to predicting this level of performance from the Bears. It also gives us a chance to look at our predictions for the remaining games and how confident we may now be feeling in those predictions. First, here’s the Bears’ remaining schedule: Week 11 – Nov. 22 vs. New Orleans Saints, noon on FOX Week 12 – Thanksgiving Day at Detroit Lions, noon on CBS Week 13 – Dec. 6 vs. Jacksonville Jaguars, noon on FOX Week 14 – Dec. 13 at Miami Dolphins, noon on CBS Week 15 – Dec. 19, Saturday at Buffalo Bills, 7:20 p.m. on CBS Week 16 – Christmas Day, Friday, Dec. 25 – vs. Green Bay Packers, noon on Netflix Week 17 – Jan. 3 vs. Detroit Lions, 3:25 p.m. on FOX Week 18 – Jan. 10 at Minnesota Vikings, TBD And here’s our look back… Donald Gooch: I had the Bears at 12-5 on the season, so if you project out their record over the next eight games based on the first nine, the expected record is between 11-6 and 12-5, so the Bears are on pace for what I expected before the season. I expect the Bears to meet, and perhaps exceed, my preseason prediction. Jacob Infante: My expectation was that the Bears would finish the year with a similar 11-6 record to what they had in 2025. Now, my expectations are higher, especially seeing their offensive improvement and after the addition of Jeffery Simmons to the defense. Their divisional schedule will be difficult to deal with, but my expectation is now that they’ll end the season with a 12-5 record. TJ Starman: My original prediction was for the Bears to end up 11-6. I was pretty accurate with my expectations for the first half of the season, though I did ultimately trade a predicted win in week 2 vs the Vikings for actual wins against both the Eagles and Seahawks. That said, I still expect 3 more losses in the next 8 games, which would put my adjusted prediction at 12-5. Josh Sunderbruch: I had the Bears at 10-6-1 and just barely making the playoffs in May, and I had guessed 6-3 at the bye, so they’ve beaten my expectations by one win so far. I can see them going 4-4 down the stretch, for 11-6, but I’d love for it to be 5-3 (for 12-5). Either way, I see them making the playoffs but losing out on hosting a home wildcard game due to a poor record against divisional foes.

stories.title: John Harbaugh endorses Cam Skattebo’s new anti-backflip stance
stories.summary: But the Giants head coach is not going to do a backflip to celebrate no more backflips by his running back.
stories.detailText: Skattebo Harbaugh Giants John Harbaugh is celebrating Cam Skattebo’s decision to change how he reacts to scoring a touchdown. But the Giants head coach is not going to do a backflip to celebrate no more backflips by his running back. Access the Giants like never before Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers. tRY IT NOW “I support his decision, and I hope he scores a lot of touchdowns,” Harbaugh said. “I hope he gets an opportunity to prove it real soon. That’d be great.” Skattebo told The Post earlier this week that he planned to stop doing his signature backflips unless “we go to the playoffs or something.” It’s Skattebo’s cautionary response to Lions star Aidan Hutchinson’s season-ending torn ACL , which he suffered last Sunday while jumping in the air to celebrate a sack. New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh speaks at a press conference in East Rutherford, N.J., Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Robert Sabo for NY Post Giants receivers Darnell Mooney and Malachi Fields also have done backflips this season. “I thought about one guy [Skattebo] maybe to talk to, but then I found out I didn’t have to because he brought it up first,” Harbaugh said. “Yeah, that’s unfortunate [for Hutchinson]. Just knowing Aidan a little bit through Michigan, when my brother coached there, I have great respect for him. Ultimate competitor-type guy and very much of a fluke, but it’s happened before. You have to think about everything.” New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo flips after a touchdown against the Washington Commanders in East Rutherford, N.J., Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Robert Sabo for NY Post The Giants have a clean injury report and dodged a scare Friday when TE Isaiah Likely (groin) did not practice. Harbaugh called it a “minor thing” and said “he’ll be fine.” No players on the 53-man roster are listed as out, doubtful or questionable. DBs Nic Jones (knee) and Eljiah Campbell (knee) — both of whom are key special-teamers — were limited Friday participants. CB Paulson Adebo was a healthy scratch last game despite carrying the 11th-highest salary cap charge ($24.1 million) for any defensive player in the NFL this season. Adebo missed five games due to injury, returned to start against the Texans, was a backup against the Eagles and then inactive against the Commanders. “He had a really good game against the Texans,” Harbaugh said. “But we were healthy again. And so that puts him more in the backup role, and then that backup role ends up being more of a special teams type of a priority for us. And like I told him, ‘In my mind, you’re a starter in this league. And when you started here, you’ve done really well. And you’re going to have to start again.’ So when that time comes, he’s in a good place.” Adebo didn’t play any special teams snaps as CB1 last season but could be looking at kick coverage as his way back onto the field eventually. OG Daniel Faalele, whom the Giants traded to the Jaguars in August for a 2027 sixth-round pick, has played 10 snaps on offense and 26 on special teams over four games for his new team.

stories.title: 2026 Week 11 rooting guide for Cowboys fans
stories.summary: The Cowboys are technically in playoff contention, so we’re tracking it
stories.detailText: Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images Outside of Dallas dropping their game to the 49ers, a lot went right for the Cowboys in Week 10. We need that to keep going for the rest of the season, both for the NFC East contention and our admittedly razor-thin hopes of a Plan B in the wild card race. A Cowboys upset over San Francisco sure would’ve been nice given how other games unfolded. The Giants getting upset by the Commanders and Green Bay getting crushed at home by Minnesota were not expected. These results helped keep a division title and the seventh seed in range, one of which is required for Dallas to still get into the playoffs. Granted, that NFC East crown is far more reachable than a wild card spot. But a lot can happen over the next eight weeks, especially as some of these NFC North and West teams start beating each other up in divisional games. A lane could still open for the Cowboys, even if we’re not good enough to use it. Current 2026 NFC Playoff Standings 1. San Francisco 49ers 8-1 (5-1 vs NFC) 2. Detroit Lions 7-2 (4-1) 3. New York Giants 5-3-1 (3-3-1) 4. Carolina Panthers 4-5 (4-3) 5. Minnesota Vikings 7-2 (5-1) 6. Chicago Bears 7-2 (5-2) 7. Green Bay Packers 6-4 (4-4) _______________________________ 8. Seattle Seahawks 6-4 (2-3) 9. Los Angeles Rams 6-4 (4-2) 10. Dallas Cowboys 4-6 (2-5) The next two weeks are critical for Dallas, getting two gifts from the scheduling gods in the Titans and Eagles. At a combined 3-15, they’re arguably the worst teams in each conference. If the Cowboys don’t come out of this stretch at 6-6, then talking about anything but the next offseason becomes quite silly. Aside from avoiding supreme embarrassment against Tennessee, what else do we need for the Cowboys from Week 11? NFC East teams Jaguars d. Giants Bengals d. Commanders Eagles d. Steelers Obviously, we need another loss for the Giants. And while we appreciate Washington helping us out there last week, we don’t need them going on some late run and becoming another problem in the division. Philadelphia is different. They seem truly done for this season, so now it’s more about not wanting them to get a top-tier draft pick. And this week, it’d be especially nice if they could upset Pittsburgh, who owes Dallas their fourth-round pick next April. NFC vs. NFC Saints d. Bears Bucs d. Lions 49ers d. Vikings It’d be great for Dallas if one team was clearly running away with the NFC North, but this feels like it’s going to be a tight battle through Week 18. As such, we need as many losses as possible for those teams so they stop monopolizing the wild card spots. Green Bay is on their bye week, so no help there. But as long as this thing stays tight, there’s a good chance that someone falls out of the playoff scene. Of course, for Dallas to benefit, they’ll also need to get past the Rams and Seahawks. Both of them are also on a bye, so we’ll see if the Cowboys can inch closer this week and then take a fresh look at playoff implications for Thanksgiving weekend. NFC vs. AFC Ravens d. Panthers Chiefs d. Cardinals If the Cowboys do win the NFC East, it’d be nice to be the third seed. We don’t really care who wins the NFC South, so long as they have a worse record than us. Carolina is the current leader, so that’s an easy pick. The Arizona-KC game is mostly meaningless. The Cardinals’ head-to-head win over Dallas shouldn’t matter by Week 18. At this point, more teams filling up the bottom of the standings, and potentially keeping the Eagles or Commanders away from the top picks, is something to root for.
