stories.detailText: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 06: Riley Moss #21 of the Denver Broncos celebrates with teammates after an interception during the third quarter against the Las Vegas Raiders at Empower Field At Mile High on October 06, 2024 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Now that Riley Moss is locked down long-term he will be Robin to Pat Surtain being Batman for years to come. That he has been able to hold up opposite of the best cornerback in the NFL is a testament to him. It’s not easy being the guy every offense looks to exploit because the guy on the other side is just too good. Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph touched on the extension and why Moss was so deserving of it. “I’ll start with this, he’s always been very athletic,” Joseph said on Thursday. “He’s competitive. To play opposite of Pat Surtain, that’s a tough job. Outside of Bo Nix on gameday, it’s probably Riley. So that part he showed from Day One. Obviously, year-by-year as he played, he’s playing cleaner football. He’s played well this year. He’s been nicked a little bit as far as missing some games, but he’s playing good ball.” He went on to dig into what makes Moss such a vital long-term piece for Denver’s defense. “No one understands his gameday because Pat’s out there at left corner, and they never look at Pat,” Joseph explained. “They do sometimes, but mostly they don’t. They’re trying to find Riley. So that’s a tough job. He’s the perfect personality for that job. Most corners wouldn’t have the resolve to kind of over, and over again just take 12 targets a game, and two penalties here and there. He’s competing. As a player, if something bad happens, he can come back in five seconds. I’m still shook by it, but Riley [says], ‘Coach, I’m good.’ I’m like, ‘Really?’ That’s a superpower. He is resilient, and he’s one of us.” Those words ‘perfect personality’ stuck out to me in every way. And like VJ said, none of us can understand what his gameday is like. To be targeted over and over again and have to battle through the mistakes that any human would make if given enough tries to make one. Just heading VJ say those things has actually made my appreciation for what Moss goes through week in and week out grow a bit more. More importantly, he has cleaned up aspects of his game. He still has a few penalties against him, but most of them are garbage calls anyway. What Riley Moss does for this defense cannot be understated. I’m glad they’ve got him locked in long-term. Broncos daily recap No Bull Perspective: The Importance of Riley Moss I’m honestly surprised at how many comments I’ve seen since Riley Moss’ extension that are casting shade on Moss, the extension, or Moss’ play. I think the biggest obstacle to understanding this extension and player comes from how hard it is to understand the role of cornerbacks in the NFL. So let’s start there. Broncos vs Raiders 5 questions: How is Raider Nation feeling about Fernando Mendoza? Fernando Mendoza made his first career NFL start for the Raiders. Now he gets a taste of the rivalry with the Broncos. Why extending Riley Moss was a smart decision for the Denver Broncos The Denver Broncos continued their tradition of rewarding their homegrown talent. Yesterday, news broke that the Broncos had agreed to terms with fourth-year cornerback Riley Moss on a four-year contract worth $67 million. As of now, the guarantees have not been made available. However, the average annual value makes him the NFL’s 23rd highest paid corner. In my opinion, that’s quite the bargain. Scouting the Enemy: Las Vegas Raiders The Denver Broncos battle the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. Here is a deeper look at their Week 11 opponent. Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph praises Riley Moss for his resilience and toughness On the day Riley Moss was extended, Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph had glowing praise for the fourth-year cornerback. Broncos aim to hit their stride at just the right time The Broncos look to carry momentum from the bye and look to build on their success as the season enters the stretch run. Potent quotables Vance Joseph On CB Riley Moss’s contract extension and the significance of keeping him in Denver long-term “It’s special. I think it speaks to the [Walton-Penner Family] Ownership [Group], the GM [General Manager George Paton] and the Head Coach [Sean Payton]. That’s the program. That’s the plan here to draft, develop and retain. So it’s working to obviously maintain and get better each year. That’s the key to this league. Keep your own, and find them early and pay them.” On maintaining a dominant defense year-to-year “It’s a standard. It’s a standard of how you work, and how you gameplan and how you play on gameday. Having great depth obviously. We’ve had some injuries, and guys stepped up and played well for us. It’s tough in this league to play really, really good year-to-year because teams obviously change. Once they get you on tape for three years, they kind of adjust to you. So making the right changes and keeping the core guys intact is key. We’ve lost some guys, but we’re finding new guys and that’s key also. For us this year, it’s been more about the explosive plays. That’s disappointing for me right now, but we’re going to fix that. I’m looking forward to us playing better football because it hasn’t been to my standard yet or our standard yet.” Darren Rizzi On S Devon Key making big plays on both defense and special teams against Carolina “The first thing I’ll say is I don’t know if I’ve been a part now, this is 18 years from the NFL… Very few times I’ve seen a guy get a game ball in two areas in one game. So No. 1, that’s a huge accomplishment and kudos to him for that. The thing that I want to say about Devon, probably the thing that’s most impressive for me is that no matter how big his role is on defense, he does not want a diminished role on special teams. He is adamant about that with me. I know my role stepped up here, but I’m still doing ‘X’, ‘Y’ and ‘Z’. I’m still doing these jobs. We do a good job of keeping the rep count, making sure it doesn’t get too high or out of control during the game. I have a ton of respect for him. I’m not surprised at his success. I just watch his work ethic, his preparation. So to get an opportunity to make a play, again, not surprised just because I know the player, the football I.Q. and the work ethic. So really, really happy for him. An incredible accomplishment to get a game ball. I think officially he got credited for two, we had him for three tackles on special teams and plus the interception. Just a really, really great job by him.” On what the Raiders special teams unit is doing well “They’ve really done a nice job. They got obviously a whole new staff. [Special Teams Coordinator] Joe DeCamillis, who’s a name that’s recognized around here. Obviously he’s been a long time NFL special teams coordinator. I have a ton of respect for Joe. I’ve known Joe for a long time. Ironically, he was actually at Texas with my son a few years ago. So I think it starts with coaching. When you watch them on film, a huge emphasis in the phases. Then obviously the players, [Raiders RB] Dylan Laube’s having a phenomenal year as a kick returner, kind of leads the league. It’s not just the 95-yard touchdown. I feel like every time we watch the plays of the week, 40-yard return, 50-yard return, he’s got these chunk plays. Downhill runner, really tough, breaks tackles. So he’s done a really good job there. [P] AJ Cole’s been one of the best punters in our league for the last five years or so. Not only is he punting the ball well, they’re covering well. So Joe’s done a really phenomenal job. I think [Head Coach] Klint [Kubiak], obviously I was with Klint in New Orleans. I think Klint has given Joe time to prepare, giving them the right pieces. So I think it comes down to a combination, but they’re doing a couple things really, really well. They do some unique things as well, so we have to be prepared. Some things we haven’t seen yet this year. So this is going to be a huge challenge for us. So kudos to them. I think this will be one of our toughest tests yet this year in this phase.” On Seahawks WR Tory Horton’s kickoff return play last week against Las Vegas and when they review situational plays like that “First of all, phenomenal heads-up play by them. Great coaching by the Seattle staff. It’s actually that particular situation we had just covered two weeks earlier. It wasn’t the tip back, but it was the time scenario. Obviously they’re trying to keep one of the timeouts, trying to keep their opposition from getting the timeout there. So if you guys remember back last year, there was a play in the Chicago game. I think it was Week 1, a very similar play where the ball came out of the end zone and it kind of stole a timeout. So we keep hitting those. Now that we’re seeing the ball in play 80 percent of the time, all these things are coming up. There was also a great play in the Washington game. Was it [Commanders WR Luke] McCaffrey, he made a really good play on the sideline where he got himself out of bounds, touched the ball. Those are huge plays. They’re chunk plays because now the ball is at the 40 [-yard line] or you burn a timeout. So yes, situation. Our big day for that is Saturday. We kind of take about a half hour or so on Saturdays and review all those situations. So we’ll certainly show those couple plays, but just constantly going through the game management part of it. I had a similar play a few years ago on a long field goal. [Former Dolphins WR] Jarvis Landry in Miami saved the field goal from going out of bounds and got a return. Now he didn’t score. He got about a 30, 40 yarder. So I’ve seen that happen before. Then [former NFL RB] Cordarrelle Patterson, he was kind of famous for trying to keep the ball in play. A lot of people didn’t realize you could bat the ball back forward and kind of keep it alive from going out of bounds. So now phenomenal play by Horton, phenomenal play by Seattle. We have our situational day on Saturdays where we kind of review all the things that could come up maybe once a season or once every five seasons, if you will.” Davis Webb On finding more efficiency in the run game “It’s a combination of a couple things. I think we can hit them with the variables and run with more conviction. We can do a better job of handling the fronts that we have, and dominating the five- and six-man boxes, and getting downhill, and being satisfied with five-, six-yard gains and getting a little bit more explosive after that. We’ve done a good job this year of not running too many negative runs. We haven’t had negative one, twos. I know there were a couple last week, but for the most part of the last nine games, there haven’t been many of those. We’ve been on track, but we can definitely do a better job of getting to second-and-5 as opposed to second-and-8 and second-and-9 and be a in a better position on second down.” On the offense putting up more points and the next step “I think it’s a combination of a few things. Our defense is doing a good job getting us the ball in short-field positions and us capitalizing. I think we’ve done a good job. Other than last week, I think there’s a three week stretch where we were close to, if not 100 percent in red zone. So dominating that and getting touchdowns as opposed to three points. Those two combinations have been really good. I think we’re playing complementary right now. Again the schedule’s going to get a little tougher here pretty soon, and we have to continue to get going.” On how they can improve on third-and-long “First of all, first and second down. Easy answer. When we are in those situations, I think it’s important to get better in a hurry. That can be protection, that can be route depth, that can be trusting your eyes in the pocket. I just named three things. It’s a combination. It really is. I think we’re getting the plays in good enough, and we’re doing a good job identifying pressures. However just kind of being 11 [players] as one a little bit better on seven-plus [yards] is important because we haven’t been good enough there.” Riley Moss Opening statement ”I’ll start by saying I’m just very thankful. I’m very thankful to be in Denver. I’m thankful for [Owner] Carrie [Walton Penner], and for [Owner & CEO] Greg [Penner], for [General Manager] George [Paton] and [Head Coach] Sean [Payton] believing in me. What they’re building is really special, and I wanted to be a part of it, and I want to be a part of it as long as I can. It’s filled with great people here in the facility. That’s the biggest thing. They’re always going after good people, and it’s easy to build a good team around really good people. I want to thank them. I want to thank my parents because I wouldn’t be where I’m at without them. They believed even when it got dark and sometimes I wouldn’t believe. There are a lot of people I want to thank. My teammates especially, I wouldn’t be able to do my job without them. I’ll open it up to questions.” On why signing a contract extension now was the right move “The biggest thing for me is fit, the people around me. I let my agent handle that stuff, and what he thought is best fit and best for me. I trust him. He’s amazing. I’m glad we were able to get this done, but the biggest thing is not being satisfied. I was just talking to ‘Court’ (WR Courtland Sutton) in the weight room. Just talking about that feeling of it’s really cool to get this money and stuff, but there’s also work to be done. How do you manage feeling happy for yourself, but also knowing you have to go out and play well against the Raiders on Sunday? It’s the 24-hour rule just like after a win. I’m going to enjoy it, but there’s still a lot of work to do.” On the mentality that has allowed him to embrace the challenge of playing opposite of CB Pat Surtain II “I think the biggest thing is it’s how I was raised with my parents. The biggest thing was they let me fail so I would be able to figure out how to become successful through that, through that adversity. It’s the reason I am who I am today. It’s a hard job, but it’s a rewarding job and I love it.” On the support of the Walton-Penner Family Ownership Group “It’s crazy because this is all I’ve ever known. I hear stories from some of my friends who are on other teams, and they say their training room isn’t even close to what they had in college. That’s crazy because here it’s, ‘Is it going to help us win?’ Then they’re going to try to invest and help us with that. That’s why we’ve been able to grow so fast as a team and as a club is [Owner & CEO] Greg [Penner] and [Owner] Carrie [Walton Penner] really caring about us as players and creating that culture, that family culture.” Under the radar The #Colts have released QB Daniel Jones, per the team. — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) November 20, 2026 In the 70s about 1/3 of all NFL games ended with a margin of 16 or more. stories.title: 49ers had enough to worry about — then Vikings got Kirk Cousins
stories.summary: PLAYBOOK: SAN FRANCISCO 49ERS (8-1) VS. MINNESOTA VIKINGS (7-2), 5:20 P.M. SUNDAY, MEXICO CITY The 49ers were already going to learn something about themselves Sunday night in Mexico City. Then...
stories.detailText: PLAYBOOK : SAN FRANCISCO 49ERS (8-1) VS. MINNESOTA VIKINGS (7-2), 5:20 P.M. SUNDAY, MEXICO CITY The 49ers were already going to learn something about themselves Sunday night in Mexico City. Then the Vikings went and got Kirk Cousins. Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) looks on during the fourth quarter against the Green Bay Packers in Green Bay, Wis., Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect What had the makings of a classic confrontation between San Francisco’s offense and Minnesota’s defense suddenly became something considerably more revealing. The Vikings have a quarterback their head coach trusts, throwing to receivers he knows, with a defense capable of carrying a team deep into January. For the 49ers, that makes this a timely examination of where they stand among the NFC’s best. They will arrive in Mexico City with an offense averaging a league-leading 399.8 yards and 31.2 points per game, second in the NFL. Minnesota counters by allowing a league-low 14 points per game and 273.3 yards, second fewest. The deeper numbers reinforce the matchup. The 49ers lead the league in offensive points per possession at three. The Vikings allow a league-low 1.24 points per possession. Something has to give. Kyle Shanahan has the personnel and imagination to make even a good defense look uncomfortable. Brock Purdy can distribute the ball to multiple threats, and Christian McCaffrey’s ability to move between the backfield and the passing game forces opponents to account for him wherever he lines up. Brian Flores has spent the season making quarterbacks uncomfortable before they even take the snap. His fronts invite questions about who is coming, who is dropping and how much time the quarterback will have to sort through it. Watching those two work against each other would have justified the trip by itself. But Cousins’ return changes the demands on San Francisco’s defense, too. Minnesota acquired him from the Raiders last week and immediately put him back in an offense he operated under Kevin O’Connell in 2022 and 2023. Five days after the trade, Cousins threw for 207 yards and two touchdowns in a 30-10 win at Green Bay. Brock Purdy (13) of the San Francisco 49ers looks to pass against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. Getty Images There was an interception mixed in. There will be adjustments as he catches up with everything that has changed since he left. Still, the Vikings suddenly look capable of making an opponent pay for devoting its entire week to figuring out their defense. Cousins understands O’Connell’s expectations. He knows how Justin Jefferson sees coverage and where Jordan Addison can hurt it. Those relationships give Minnesota a chance to accelerate a transition that normally requires considerably more time. And they give the 49ers a second problem to solve. San Francisco just scored 46 points against Dallas and needed nearly every one of them. Allowing 40 points in a victory leaves plenty to address, especially with O’Connell getting another week to prepare his reunited offense. The 49ers can welcome that challenge. Their 8-1 record has earned them a place near the front of the conference. Beating a 7-2 Minnesota team with this defense and a familiar quarterback settling back in would provide another reason to believe they can stay there. San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan, left, and general manager John Lynch watch players warm up on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, in Arlington, Texas. AP Photo/Julio Cortez Sunday offers the kind of opponent that can expose a weakness while there is still time to fix it. Or confirm that the 49ers have fewer of them than almost everyone else. MARQUEE MATCHUP S 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan vs. Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores Two coaches operating at the top of their games will spend Sunday trying to take away what makes the other so effective. Shanahan wants Purdy playing with clarity, using motion, formations and the threat of the run to create favorable throws. Flores wants that picture changing, preferably after Purdy has committed to what he thinks he sees. McCaffrey could determine who gets his way. Sending him into a route gives Purdy another dangerous option. Keeping him in protection helps account for the pressure Flores brings. Shanahan’s challenge is preserving enough receiving options to punish Minnesota’s aggression. For Flores, it is forcing quick decisions without making the answers obvious. Every protection adjustment and late defensive movement will have a purpose. Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell vs. 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris O’Connell and Morris helped the Rams win a Super Bowl following the 2021 season, with O’Connell coordinating the offense and Morris running the defense. Those practice field confrontations now become part of the preparation for a game with considerable NFC implications. O’Connell has his quarterback back, and with Cousins comes the freedom to call plays knowing how the man executing them will respond. That familiarity makes Minnesota feel more complete. Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell looks on after a game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis., Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Morris understands how O’Connell builds an offense and how its concepts fit together. He can use that knowledge to challenge Cousins’ first read and force him to hold the ball. O’Connell will anticipate those adjustments, of course. That is what makes this compelling. Two former colleagues know how much the other knows, and both must decide when to break their tendencies. THE PICK Vikings 31, 49ers 28 Something feels right about Cousins finding his way back to Minnesota after 2 ½ seasons away, with his recovery from the Achilles injury that ended his 2023 season part of that journey. He returns to a more complete team, with a defense capable of giving him a chance to finish what he started. The 49ers will make Minnesota earn every bit of this. But with another week alongside O’Connell, Cousins makes enough timely throws, and Flores finds one late stop to give the reunion another memorable chapter. KEY STAT : 8 The Vikings sacked Jordan Love eight times in Cousins’ return last Sunday. Purdy’s protection will face a considerably tougher test than the reunion storyline alone suggests.

stories.title: Fernando Mendoza’s tests not getting any easier. Broncos will show how much rookie learned
stories.summary: PLAYBOOK: LAS VEGAS RAIDERS (4-6) AT DENVER BRONCOS (7-2), 1:25 P.M. SUNDAY Fernando Mendoza compared what Mike Macdonald did to him Sunday to playing chess. He left out the part...
stories.detailText: PLAYBOOK : LAS VEGAS RAIDERS (4-6) AT DENVER BRONCOS (7-2), 1:25 P.M. SUNDAY Fernando Mendoza compared what Mike Macdonald did to him Sunday to playing chess. He left out the part about the chessboard being set up inside an octagon. The Seahawks’ defensive wizard of a head coach challenged the Raiders rookie with shifting coverages and pressure packages, then let his defenders deliver the physical consequences. There were punches, a little taekwondo and enough swift kicks to leave Mendoza studying the board from the canvas. Fernando Mendoza (15) of the Las Vegas Raiders warms up before a game at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images Six sacks will do that. Now comes Denver, where another accomplished defensive coach and a rested collection of pass rushers await his second NFL start. Welcome to the NFL, the sequel. Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph has had the bye week to prepare for the Raiders. Macdonald just provided fresh film of what confused Mendoza, what slowed his decisions and what happened when an encouraging first half gave way to a miserable second. Joseph will have his own ways of asking whether the rookie learned anything. That is how this works. Put a weakness on film and the next opponent will make you prove you have addressed it. Fix that one and someone will start looking for another. Mendoza understood as much after his debut, accepting responsibility for the sacks and acknowledging that Macdonald had fooled him. His willingness to own those mistakes was encouraging. Sunday offers the first opportunity to show what he has done about them. There was plenty worth building on. Brock Bowers #89 and Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders bump fists on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas. Getty Images Mendoza completed 11 of 13 passes for 90 yards in the first half against Seattle, distributing the ball to eight receivers and scoring on a 10-yard quarterback draw. He looked comfortable enough to give the Raiders reason to believe they could win. Then Seattle adjusted. Mendoza finished the second half 6-of-16 passing, and the Raiders struggled to sustain anything. The challenge in Denver is recognizing those changes quickly enough to keep the offense moving. That means identifying pressure, trusting the appropriate answer and understanding when a play has reached its expiration date. It also means getting considerably more help. The Raiders rushed for 65 yards on 24 attempts against Seattle. Asking a rookie to keep solving difficult passing situations while the running game produces so little is an exhausting way to develop a quarterback. Klint Kubiak has to find ways to create manageable downs, move Mendoza when the situation calls for it and give him throws he can make decisively. The offensive line must provide enough time for those decisions to matter. Denver has won five straight games, and Nik Bonitto supplied a reminder of its ability to finish opponents with his late strip-sack against Carolina before the bye. Mendoza is walking into another difficult classroom, with the crowd adding to the demands. Someday, he might look back on these first two starts with a debt of gratitude. The lessons could help him recognize trouble sooner, play faster and become the quarterback the Raiders envisioned. For now, he would probably appreciate learning a few of them without another black eye. MARQUEE MATCHU PS Broncos edge rusher Nik Bonitto vs. Raiders left tackle Kolton Miller Miller has not been as sharp as the Raiders have come to expect, and this would be a good week to rediscover his best football. Bonitto remains one of the league’s most dangerous rushers, even with his sack production trailing the pace of his recent seasons. His strip-sack against Carolina showed how quickly he can decide a game, and the bye provided time to recharge for the stretch run. Las Vegas Raiders players celebrate Fernando Mendoza’s touchdown against the Seattle Seahawks in Las Vegas, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Seattle won 21-13. Getty Images Miller must handle Bonitto’s speed without becoming vulnerable to his counters. Mendoza can help by getting the ball out on time and maintaining his position in the pocket. But the Raiders need their veteran left tackle to win enough individual battles to give their rookie a chance. Raiders cornerback Eric Stokes vs. Broncos receiver Jaylen Waddle Stokes needs a response game after an uneven season took a conspicuous turn against Seattle. Kubiak briefly pulled him after plays on which the coach said his effort fell short. The message was clear. A player the Raiders trust to handle difficult coverage assignments still has to finish every down. Waddle can make any lapse expensive. His speed puts pressure on a cornerback’s positioning, and his ability to create separation demands concentration throughout the route. Stokes must stay disciplined when Bo Nix extends plays and keep competing if the ball goes elsewhere. The Raiders’ pass rush also has to finish its work. Against Denver’s most dangerous receiver, coverage and effort will both be under scrutiny. THE PICK Broncos 31, Raiders 21 Mendoza looks more comfortable in his second start, gets the ball out faster and throws his first NFL touchdown pass. There will be enough improvement to give the Raiders something tangible to build on. But their inability to establish a running game keeps putting too much on the rookie, and the defense gives Denver too many opportunities to answer. Coming off the bye, the Broncos have the preparation time and pass rush to force mistakes. Mendoza takes a step forward. The Raiders still come up short. KEY STAT : 11 That many Seahawks defenders pressured Mendoza in his first start, illustrating how much the Raiders must improve their protection before facing Denver’s varied rush.

stories.title: Back at practice again, Bengals QB Burrow optimistic he'll be at full strength
stories.summary: A full participant at practice for the second straight day despite the bug that he has battled, Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow is optimistic that he'll be at full strength when Cincinnati plays the Washington Commanders on "Monday Night Football."
stories.detailText: CINCINNATI -- With hushed tones and a plaid orange-and-black beanie nearly pulled over his eyes, Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow was limited in his comments about the illness ailing him ahead of Monday's game against the Washington Commanders . But importantly, Burrow was optimistic that he'll be at full strength when Cincinnati plays in its second primetime game and third showcase game in as many weeks. "Getting better," Burrow said after Friday's practice. The injury report confirmed Burrow's comments, too. He was a full participant for the second straight day despite the bug that he has battled in recent days. Typically, Burrow talks to reporters following the first practice of the game week. But given his condition, the team bumped him an extra day as he tries to recover. Wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase took his place instead and had a little fun with the switch. He wore Burrow's practice jersey to his news conference, opened with Burrow's trademark greeting (either one or two "hellos") and even answered a couple of questions as if he was Burrow. But when it came time to get serious, Chase felt like Burrow was still in good shape. "Overall, he looks good," Chase said Thursday. "I think everybody around the team is coming down with a little sickness. But overall, he still looks good, still feels the same." Various members of the team have felt ill in recent days, starting with right guard Dalton Risner , who was added to the injury report shortly before the team's 38-18 win against the Pittsburgh Steelers last Sunday night. Risner eventually left the game because of knee injuries and has not practiced yet this week. Burrow isn't the only starter this week who is under the weather. Cornerback Dax Hill missed his second straight practice as he also battles an illness. Myles Hinton , a backup tackle, returned to practice after being sick on Thursday. Burrow's proven strategy to get better: sleep, hydrate and eat spicy foods. And it helps that Cincinnati (7-2) has an extra day to prepare for the Commanders (3-5-1) given how the players have felt physically. "A lot of sick guys early in the week, so I don't know if the energy would've been there if we were a Sunday game coming in on Wednesday," Burrow said. "But we had three days off. It was a little lower yesterday, guys coming off of that, but today guys got after it and we're ready to go." The "Monday Night Football" contest will also mark Burrow's first regular-season game at Washington since 2020, since he suffered a season-ending ACL injury in his rookie season, an event that feels like a lifetime ago. "It's been a long time," Burrow said. "It is crazy. This season has gone by quickly and the last six years have gone by very quickly. A lot has happened for sure."

stories.title: The Colts cut QB Daniel Jones. Should the Cardinals make a claim?
stories.summary: Could Jones become the starter going forward?
stories.detailText: HOUSTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 19: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts throws a pass against the Houston Texans during the first quarter of the game at Reliant Stadium on November 19, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Arizona Cardinals are one of the league’s worst teams this year. Another bad team, the Indianapolis Colts just released their starting quarterback, Daniel Jones. Should the Cardinals make a waiver wire claim? Before Jones was released, he had trade value. The waiver wire is situated where the worst team has the first dibs, then the second worst, and so on. RELATED: CARDINALS DRAFT PICKS HAVE FAILED TO MAKE AN IMPACT The current order is: 1 Tennessee Titans (1-8-0) 2 Los Angeles Chargers (1-8-0) 3 Miami Dolphins (1-8-0) 4 New York Jets (2-8-0) 5 Philadelphia Eagles (2-7-0) 6 Indianapolis Colts (3-8-0) 7 Arizona Cardinals (3-7-0) 8 Atlanta Falcons (3-7-0) This means that the Cardinals are seventh in line. The Titans drafted Cam Ward last year, the Chargers have Justin Herbert, Miami spent big bucks on Malik Willis in last year’s free agency period, and Geno Smith for the Jets is back into the fold. The big question might be for Arizona is if they grabbed Jones off waivers, would he become the default starter or just another stallion in the QB stable? Would he play, or sit until Carson Beck becomes injured, frustrated, or incapable of assuming the starting role? While with the Colts, Jones was under a two-year $88 million deal. Here is the QB status of each team: Titans: Ward is doing okay considering the offensive line is weak. The team has a capable backup in Mitch Trubisky. Chargers: LA got their first win with Herbert still under center. His backup, Trey Lance, is on IR which means QB3 D.J. Uiagalelei is now Herbert’s backup. Dolphins: Willis is on IR with Kyle McCord starting and Brady Cook his backup. Jets: Starter Geno Smith has just returned from IR. Rookie Cade Klubnik is his backup. Eagles: We are all aware that starter Jalen Hurts is on IR and gone for the year. In his place is Joe Milton who isn’t exactly tearing up the league. Tanner McKee and Cole Payton are backups. With the Colts picking at #6, they are out. The Titans look good along with the Jets. But the remainder could use Jones. So could Arizona. Jones was taken with the sixth overall selection in the 2019 NFL Draft by the New York Football Giants after a standout career at Duke. He was supposed to be the future after Eli Manning retired. In 2022, Jones made NFL history by becoming the first player ever with 300+ passing yards, 2+ touchdown passes, and 70+ rushing yards in a playoff game. The next year, Jones inked a four-year $160 million extension, but had a knee injury in Week 9. Late in 2024, he was benched for undrafted Tommy DeVito who set the New York area on fire as an Italian-American quarterback who was winning games and his downhome attitude. In late November, the Giants shocked everyone by releasing Jones. He spent one season with the Minnesota Vikings before hooking on with the Colts in 2025 who signed him to a one-year $14 million deal and competed with Anthony Richardson for the starting role. Jones tore his Achilles tendon late in the season and landed on IR. +2 for the Terminator 😤 📺: @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/TzcavjrlrF — Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) November 20, 2026 This season, he was named the starter for Week 1. Jones started all 11 games for a listless offensive unit which has been selling off their key players. Their offensive line is absolutely porous. This year, Jones hasn’t had any time to throw and has paltry production such as 144 (twice) yards, 108 (twice), 143, and 166 in games. He has thrown seven touchdowns against 13 interceptions. For his eight-year career, Jones’ stats: 94 games with 93 starts, 1,903 completions on 2,976 attempts for 19,657 yards, converted 979 first downs, 96 TDs, 68 picks, a 63.9% completion ratio, sacked 257 times, an 84.1 QB rating, and a 35-57-1 starting win-loss record. He is a very good runner with 478 carries for 2,441 yards with another 21 scores. Gooooooould 💨 📺 Prime pic.twitter.com/YmZXB3NfsN — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) November 20, 2026 Thursday night, the Colts lost to the then-3-6-0 Houston Texans 26-3 in a totally lopsided contest. Indy had 38 rushing yards while Jones went 12 for 27 for 144 yards, sacked twice and had a single pick with zero TDs. The Colts’ offense is ranked #30 in the league. They have allowed the eighth most sacks (28) and thrown the most interceptions with 13. Despite losing one of the best offensive guards in the league by trading away LG Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks before the trade deadline, the Indianapolis offensive line is ranked #17. By claiming Jones, it could mean the Cardinals would have a capable quarterback for their remaining games this season who would compete with Gardner Minshew and Carson Beck in training camp next year. Then again, what would be the cost to bring him in? None of the four quarterbacks on the roster are costing the franchise hardly anything.

stories.title: Daniel Jones has been released by the Colts. Should the Patriots go after him?
stories.summary: Why the Patriots should, and shouldn’t, sign Daniel Jones after his release from the Colts.
stories.detailText: You heard about a Friday news dump, but have you heard about a Friday QB dump? That’s precisely what the Indianapolis Colts did when they released their starting quarterback , Daniel Jones, earlier today. Jones, 29, was in his second season with the franchise and just eight months removed from signing a two-year, $88 million contract extension. However, he and the Colts as a whole have struggled mightily this year, leading to some sweeping changes within the organization. First, they fired the GM who signed him to that deal, Chris Ballard, and now they let go of Jones himself. His release comes with the Colts at 3-8 and Jones having completed 205 of 351 pass attempts (58.4%) for 1,974 yards with seven touchdowns and 13 interceptions. A year removed from tearing his Achilles tendon, he is ranked 30th among 31 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA per play this season (-0.139) and 31st in both net yards per attempt (4.8) and completion percentage above expectation (-6.1). Long story short, he has been dreadful. And yet, the New England Patriots might just keep a close eye on him. The Patriots, after all, saw their own starting QB, Drake Maye, suffer a fractured fibula during last Sunday’s loss versus the Detroit Lions. While it remains to be seen how long he will be out, Maye missing most if not all of his team’s seven final regular season games this year would not come as a surprise. The question now becomes whether or not the Patriots should pursue Jones as a replacement. Let’s make the argument in favor of and against such a move. Why the Patriots should sign Daniel Jones Before making this argument, it needs to be prefaced with this: everything in this section only applies to Jones going through the waiver wire unclaimed and making it to the open market. According to Jason Fitzgerald of Over the Cap, a team would need $6.35 million in salary cap space to claim Jones — financial flexibility the Patriots do not have at the moment. If he passes waivers, he could be signed to a deal worth as little as $505,554. With that out of the way, let’s take a look at why brining Jones in would make sense for the Patriots. It all starts with one question: would he be an upgrade over Tommy DeVito for however long Drake Maye will be sidelined? His play this season so far suggests that that might not be the case. However, a change in environment might help Jones regain some of the confidence he had in his first year with the Colts, when he played some of the best football of his career and finished the season sixth in the league in EPA per play (0.201). If the Patriots can get a fraction of that, they should be happy with Jones as a better alternative than DeVito. In addition, Jones also has some familiarity with the Patriots scheme. While he never played directly under offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, he did spend the better part of three seasons under former New England assistant Brian Daboll. The offense Daboll ran with the Giants has similarities to McDaniels’ in terms of terminology, quarterback responsibility and play designs, meaning that the lead-up time for Jones to get ready would be comparatively small. Inserting Jones would likely also not come with significant philosophical changes. In essence, after all, he is a similar player type as Maye is: somebody capable of making plays with his arm as well as his legs, as evidenced by his career rushing average of 6.1 yards per carry. While his highs have not been close to Maye’s, he has shown that he can be an adequate NFL starting quarterback and somebody able to elevate the talent around him. That obviously was not the case in Indianapolis this season, but if a change of scenery and move to a better-run team can get him close to that, it would be precisely what the Patriots need right now if there are any doubts about DeVito. And even if not, what do the Patriots have to lose? They are 5-5 and fighting for their playoff lives, and signing Jones would not automatically disqualify them from starting DeVito. At the very least, he would provide veteran depth better suited to challenge the post-Maye hierarchy than sixth-round rookie Behren Morton. Why the Patriots shouldn’t sign Daniel Jones On Friday, Jones became the first quarterback in the NFL in more than three decades to get released less than 24 hours after starting a game. That plus the fact the Colts are willing to cut their losses despite the financial investment they made in him just this offseason should tell you all you need to know. It’s been bad this year. Very, very bad. While there might be a snowballing effect to Jones’ struggles and a fresh start could indeed help him regain the form he previously showed, there is no denying he has played some of the worst football in the NFL this year. The numbers mentioned above are an illustration of that. Some of it had to do with the surroundings and a Colts team that a) lacking quality across the board, and b) is in a free fall since October. In addition, his injury situation also seems to have played a part in it: 12 months after his torn Achilles, he still does not look like he is close to 100% and fails to consistently to step into throws, maneuver the pocket and pick up yards on the ground, averaging just 3.8 yards per carry. On top of it, Jones has been a streaky player throughout his career. While there have been stretches of play where he lived up to his former first-round status, the lows have been underwhelming, including this season. Given all of that, expecting a quick turnaround in New England would be naive, particularly considering that the Patriots are missing several offensive pieces because of injury. But even if they didn’t, Jones would not have any familiarity with them: despite some experience in a McDaniels-style system, he would have to build chemistry with his receiving corps, offensive line and coaching staff on the fly. Tommy DeVito, meanwhile, has a two-year head start in that regard. Speaking of DeVito, he was signed to a contract extension in the offseason to serve as QB2 and has, by all accounts, been a model citizen deserving of his shot. Obviously, the job should go to the best option regardless of contract situation. That said, all things considered — including what a change might mean for the locker room — DeVito still has a strong case to be just that. Verdict Even though they are still in a competitive position on paper, the Patriots are fighting for their playoff lives with Drake Maye sidelined for the foreseeable future. Their margin for error, meanwhile, is, to quote safety Kevin Byard, “basically at zero.” Would adding Jones increase it and allow New England to play winning football during Maye’s absence? Ideally, that is not a question they would have to ask; Tommy DeVito stepping in and leading the offense at an adequate level would be the best-case scenario. Of course, as the Lions game showed, there is a realistic chance the lights are too bright for him. The problem is, they also might be for Jones. So far this season, after all, he has not been good and not been able to hold up to the pressure of being the guy at quarterback in Indianapolis. He wouldn’t quite be that in New England, sure, but the eyes of one of the NFL’s biggest markets would still be on him. Would that prevent the Patriots from signing him? Probably not. Still, it is one of the factors to consider alongside the arguments outlined above. And putting all of those together, it is clear the decision whether or not to sign Jones as a potential stand-in for Maye is quite nuanced. At the end of the day, Mike Vrabel, Eliot Wolf and Ryan Cowden — the latter of whom spent time with Jones in New York — will have to see their way through it. And once they do, they very well might find that the potential disruption caused by adding Jones might not be worth the theoretical gains. What do you think about Daniel Jones? Should the Patriots pursue him, or steer clear of him? Please head down to the comment section to share your thoughts, or jump into the following discussion thread set up by community member Gonzucla in the Feed.

stories.title: Cowboys changing things up in search of consistency vs. Titans
stories.summary: Are the Cowboys in for another dogfight at home this week?
stories.detailText: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images Both the Dallas Cowboys, and their closest division rival this season, the New York Giants, host opponents from the AFC South this weekend. If the Cowboys were even living up to half of the expectations of this season, this Week 11 schedule would look like a golden opportunity to separate from the Giants, as they face the 7-2 Jacksonville Jaguars while the Cowboys have the 1-8 Tennessee Titans. Instead, the Cowboys already blew an opportunity to win in the same week the Giants lost against the San Francisco 49ers. Even if the Giants do lose as home underdogs to the Jaguars, the Cowboys have invited enough added drama this week with a change of defensive play-callers to make the Titans feel like another handful of an opponent. This is especially true considering how close both other games against AFC South foes have been this year, both in the win column, but neither convincing. Getting a convincing win is something Cowboys fans simply do not have faith in their team doing at all right now, and not something the Titans have given away easily despite struggling under the new coaching of Robert Saleh and offensive coordinator Brian Daboll. Hope for the playoffs will still feel thin even with a win Dallas is expected to get against these Titans. The Cowboys have made their bed with this roster and coaching staff and will have to withstand however many embarrassing losses can come from it, with the Titans having the potential to be the worst of 2026. It is time for our weekly look at how the Cowboys avoid this loss and go into Thanksgiving with a chance at a winning streak again, or what could lead to the latest AT&T Stadium embarrassment after all. The Dallas Cowboys will beat the Tennessee Titans if… …they can throw the ball downfield. Every other week for the Cowboys passing attack seems to feel like a CeeDee Lamb feature game right now, with Lamb having a big say in the win over the Colts in week nine, but it was George Pickens’ best game of the season with three touchdowns in week ten agaisnt the 49ers. The fact we are still waiting into late November for a game where both Lamb and Pickens are established in a game plan and get going at the same time is a horrible sign for play-caller Brian Schottenheimer. Beating bad AFC teams is one thing he’s proven capable of though, and if now isn’t the time to see both Lamb and Pickens unleashed downfield, it may never come. The Titans defense is effectively tied with the Las Vegas Raiders for worst in the league in yards per passing attempt allowed. All three of their cornerbacks that led the team in snaps last week against the Jaguars are new to the team this season – Cor’Dale Flott, Alontae Taylor, and Joshua Williams. Tennessee is also the fourth worst team at getting to the quarterback this season with 14 sacks, just one more than the 49ers team the Cowboys offense scored 40 points against last week. The Cowboys defense is more of an unknown than ever before coming into this game after already underperforming all season, so the adage that Dallas can win this game by having Dak Prescott simply outplay Cam Ward by a big margin is not a reliable one. That said, another huge Prescott game against this opponent where he’s able to effectively get the ball deep to both of his top receivers should be enough to get in the win column. The Cowboys have beaten Robert Saleh defenses consistently before, and will have to do so again to keep faint NFC East hopes alive this Sunday. The Dallas Cowboys will lose to the Tennessee Titans if… …they don’t rally to the ball on defense. The football gods always seem to work in mysterious ways, in the sense they will test the very thing a team is struggling with in the blink of an eye. The Cowboys reasoning for having the veteran coach Mike Pettine take over defensive play-calling from rookie Christian Parker has more layers than an onion. One of the more sound reasons though is that the team is heavily invested financially in their front seven, where Quinnen Williams has looked more and more like a cornerstone player to build around each week in his first full season with the team. Pettine will likely look to run the defense with a front-centric mindset, focusing on this front seven first and then the backend, where as Parker was the opposite. For a coach that wasn’t here for any offseason activity at all, and only been in the building since October, his first test of this new approach comes against a challenging opponent. With last year’s first overall pick Cam Ward at quarterback, the Titans rank in the 98th percentile in their utilization of the quick passing game this season. They have yet another dual-threat, home run hitting running back in former Cowboy Tony Pollard. Ward’s best trait has always been his ability to throw the ball out of a moving pocket, and the Titans are figuring out in real time how to protect him and also target the middle of the field at a high rate to open up the sophomore passer’s game. The Titans lone win this season came in week six against the Colts, but this is what Ward’s passing chart looked like: For comparison, the Titans didn’t beat the Jaguars last week, but they put up numbers offensively and played well, and this is how Ward threw the ball to do so: If Mike Pettine is going to make a difference for the Cowboys after they just allowed a franchise record for yards given up in a home game, to a 49ers team that exposed them in the middle of the field, with a mobile QB as well, doing so against the Titans would actually be a solid start. With the ball coming out so quickly from Ward’s hands, the Cowboys likely can’t rely on the pass rush element they got against the 49ers with five sacks either. Pass rush will have to come from sound coverage in the short to intermediate part of the field, where the Titans will look to stress Shemar James, Caleb Downs, and even Rashan Gary who got up field without contain on a number of big 49ers plays last week. If the Cowboys cannot handle these things, and also struggle to get multiple bodies to Pollard in the run game and allow him to get around the edge or push the pile, it could be yet another long afternoon for Brian Schottenheimer’s team against an inferior opponent.

stories.title: Giants shocked to learn Colts cut ex-teammate Daniel Jones
stories.summary: John Harbaugh’s eyes nearly popped out of his head upon learning that the Colts cut quarterback Daniel Jones.
stories.detailText: Daniel Jones has been released by the Colts. John Harbaugh’s eyes nearly popped out of his head upon learning that the Colts cut quarterback Daniel Jones . Harbaugh wasn’t the Giants’ head coach when they stunningly cut Jones in November 2024, so they don’t have the personal relationship that Jones maintains with others in East Rutherford. But the Colts are next week’s opponent, so the Giants’ behind-the-scenes advance-scouting staffers were just thrown a major curveball. The Colts plan to start first-round draft bust Anthony Richardson , which means an offense that could be more option-based in store on Nov. 29 to hide Richardson’s passing inaccuracy. Daniel Jones has been released by the Colts. Getty Images “[It changes] probably pretty dramatically. I mean, wow,’” Harbaugh admitted. “I don’t want to get ahead of ourselves here, and you just hit me with that. But definitely the offense will be the offense that they run, but it’ll be centered around the quarterback for sure, and they’re probably different styles to some degree, so we’ll have to look at that when the time comes. We have people doing that this week. They’ll have to make a left turn, obviously.” Unlike when the Giants demoted Jones from starter to third-stringer to protect themselves against an injury clause in his contract, Jones did not ask the Colts for his release, head coach Shane Steichen said. In the Giants locker room, news of Jones’ release brought back memories. What does it say to teammates when you release the quarterback who started the first 11 games? “That the writing is on the wall for the season and you have to get through the next six games the best you can play,” right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor told The Post. “D.J. is a great guy but he’s in such a predicament. He went there last year and balled out, so it’s definitely not a ‘him’ thing. When you trade everyone like they did, it’s hard.” John Harbaugh, head coach of the Giants. Getty Images Giants backup offensive lineman Josh Sills was with the Colts last season and to start 2025. He saw the same hard-working Jones that was beloved by Giants teammates. “He helped me in any and every way imaginable,” Sills told The Post. “He went above and beyond to make sure everyone had what they needed to achieve their goals. It’s a team game. It takes 11 guys.” Anthony Richardson will now start at quarterback for the Colts. Getty Images Next week was billed as the Jones Revenge Game. Instead, Jones didn’t even make it through the first year of the two-year, $88 million contract that he signed after a torn Achilles. Jones might be able to help the Patriots or Ravens in their playoff chase. Or he could help the Eagles not be an embarrassment the rest of the season. Or use his ties to Broncos offensive coordinator Davis Webb to become the backup for a Super Bowl contender. Any team that claims him off waivers will inherit $2.1 million in salary this season and a $10.5 million injury guarantee for 2027. Returning to the Giants or reuniting with Brian Daboll in Tennessee are extremely unlikely possibilities. “I wish the best for him and I know he’s going to make the most of his next opportunity,” left tackle Andrew Thomas said. “But I’m focused on what we have going on and we’re not looking at Indy right now. We’re focused on this week and Jacksonville.”

stories.title: Police investigate man's death after alleged altercation at 49ers-Cowboys game
stories.summary: Police are investigating the death of a man who was allegedly involved in an altercation before Sunday's game between the Cowboys and 49ers at AT&T Stadium.
stories.detailText: Police are investigating the death of a man who was allegedly involved in an altercation before Sunday's game between the Dallas Cowboys and San Francisco 49ers at AT&T Stadium. According to the Tarrant County Medical Examiner's Office, Mario Narro, 36, died Wednesday in an Arlington hospital. Narro's family had contacted the Arlington Police Department on Tuesday to make a report. Police were told Narro fell during an altercation with another fan around kickoff time. He remained for the entire game, but after complaining of pain, a friend flagged down paramedics at the stadium and Narro was transported to the hospital. Police are in the early stages of the investigation and in the process of reviewing surveillance footage from AT&T Stadium. The Tarrant County Medical Examiner's Office will conduct an autopsy to determine the official cause of death. Speaking on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas on Friday, Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones said he was unaware of what happened Sunday and that he had just received information about it. "We had no record of an incident," Jones said, "and we'll be obviously looking into that."

stories.title: Steelers-Eagles preview: What to expect from Philadelphia’s offense, defense Week 11
stories.summary: It’s a battle for Pennsylvania in the NFL’s Week 11 as the 6-3 Steelers take on the 2-7 Eagles.
stories.detailText: Photo by Todd Olszewski/Getty Images | Getty Images The Steelers will travel to Philadelphia — a city where they haven’t won since 1965 — on Sunday in a game that many fans have had circled as an Eagles victory since before the season. However, the 2026 Eagles aren’t the same team that made the playoffs every year from 2021-25. They enter Week 11 with a dismal 2-7 record, with all those losses coming in a row against the Bears, Rams, Jaguars, Panthers, Cowboys, Commanders and Giants. Philadelphia hasn’t been in the win column since a Sept. 20 victory over the Titans. Is this Eagles team finally bad enough for the Steelers to break such a lengthy losing streak in The City of Brotherly Love? Or will Philadelphia, fresh off a Week 10 bye, be able to hold off the Steelers at home for yet another season? We’ll find out in Week 11. What to expect from the Eagles’ offense Rushing YPG: 88.6 (28th) Passing YPG: 171.7 (27th) PPG: 16.4 (31st) RB: It’s been a rough year for the Eagles offense, now on its third quarterback of the season ahead of Week 11’s matchup versus the Steelers. The numbers above speak for themselves: Philadelphia has struggled on both the ground and in the air in 2026, dealing with injuries, the sudden retirement of right tackle Lane Johnson, and poor execution from players on the field. The Eagles have only scored over 20 points four times this season, and have yet to break 30 once. Before a Week 10 bye, the Eagles faced the New York Giants in Week 9, falling 19-11 in an ugly game that’s been all too familiar for the Philly faithful. But one thing did change, with the Eagles trying to spark their Jalen Hurts-less offense by replacing backup Tanner McKee with Joe “Bazooka” Milton at quarterback. He’s expected to start again against Pittsburgh on Sunday. The results were not great against the Giants, with Milton finishing with 169 passing yards and 18/34 completion in Week 9. He didn’t throw a single touchdown or interception, and was sacked a whopping seven times. However, the guy with the “Bazooka” nickname does indeed have a powerful arm, with Milton logging an 11.8% deep throw percentage along with eight air yards per attempt (both team highs for the Eagles this season). He’s also a much better runner than McKee, leading the Eagles with 64 yards on the ground and a 7.1 average against New York. Frankly, Milton plays like a still-developing quarterback. He holds onto the ball too long and doesn’t seem to go through his reads at NFL speed. However, his arm talent does allow him to rifle balls into open zones when he sees them, and there’s always a little bit of worry when playing a passer with his physical abilities — even if everything only clicks a few times a game, he can still make defenses pay. It’s worth noting that Pittsburgh hasn’t played many highly-mobile quarterbacks this year, and has had some issues with deep coverage this season. With Joe Milton getting a chance to start it's a good time for us to all remember THE PASS pic.twitter.com/WNYd7j9DRd — Bill Barnwell (@billbarnwell) November 4, 2026 With Milton under center, the Eagles have mixed up their playbook from McKee a bit with a few more rollouts and designed quarterback runs. What hasn’t changed, however, is that Philadelphia remains an 11-personnel heavy team that likes short throws outside the numbers to move the ball in the passing game. Making matters worse is that despite the short passing game, Philadelphia ranks dead-last in the league in yards after catch in 2026, with just 738 on the year. First-round receiver Makai Lemon is a name to watch as a twitchy underneath target, and Milton will get to throw to the now-healthy Devonta Smith for the first time this season after the latter missed the Giants game with injury. That’s a big boost to what was a decimated Philly receiving core in Week 9. However, Dontayvion Wicks will still be out for the Eagles against Pittsburgh. Eagles WR1 DeVonta Smith pic.twitter.com/fraYBtPOtG — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) June 1, 2026 Capping the Eagles’ offensive ceiling has been a rough year from the line, which lost All-World right tackle Lane Johnson to retirement in October and has struggled with some regression. Jordan Mailata remains a very good left tackle and Philadelphia now has Landon Dickerson back from injured reserve, but the Eagles still rank seventh-highest in sack rate allowed (9%), third-highest in pressure rate allowed (41.9%), and second-highest in runs stuffed percentage (23.5%) despite facing the seventh-most light boxes in the league. Having inexperienced signal-callers since Hurts landed on injured reserve certainly hasn’t helped the Eagles in pass protection. Philadelphia struggled mightily with interior pressure against the Giants, and gave up a number of unblocked rushers on stunts and twists. One name to watch is rookie right tackle Markell Bell, a massive human being who has struggled some in pass protection this year, but is a promising run blocker. Look at the big Markell bell on this play pic.twitter.com/1GM9qoYBTf — 𝗘𝗮𝗴𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗺 (@EaglesScoutRoom) October 6, 2026 Still, on the ground, the Eagles’ inside zone-heavy attack is tied for 28th in the NFL in yards per rush (3.7), with just 28 non-Milton yards on the ground against New York. However, star running back Saquon Barkley, who played through injury against the Giants, should be rested up after the Eagles’ bye and looking a bit more explosive. In two of Barkley’s first three games this season, he averaged 5.5 yards per carry — when healthy, the 29-year-old is still a legitimate offensive weapon. After a nightmare game against the Bengals last week, the Pittsburgh defense matches up much better against Philadelphia. The key will be stifling the Eagles’ run game and pressuring Milton, which the Steelers’ front seven is certainly capable of, especially with Derrick Harmon back in play on the interior. Milton averaged 3.12 seconds to throw last week — that should give TJ Watt more time to get home against a rookie right tackle. Still, with Devonta Smith back in the lineup for the Eagles, along with solid ancillary weapons in Lemon and tight end Dallas Goedert available, a Pittsburgh secondary that got torched last week will still need to bring a better performance to the table. That said, there should be a lot more optimism heading into this week than the last for the Steelers’ defense. What to expect from the Eagles’ defense Rushing YPG: 126.1 (25th) Passing YPG: 227.3 (18th) PPG: 24.6 (19th) RP : Much like the Eagles’ offense this year, the defensive side of the ball still possesses a lot of talent, but has performed well below expectations. A unit that was the driving force behind a Super Bowl victory just two seasons ago, the Eagles seemed poised to field a young and imposing defense that would keep them contenders for the rest of the 2020s. Instead, they were sellers at the deadline, shipping away defensive tackle Jordan Davis, whom they’d signed to a three-year, $78 million extension this March. I spoke with Brandon Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation this week , to try to get a sense of why the defense has underperformed, and he said it’s been one of the more baffling developments this season. He cited a lingering injury to superstar defensive tackle Jalen Carter and a general lack of pass rush as the biggest factor. Whether or not Carter is living up to the extension he signed this past summer (four years, $152 million) is seemingly a hot topic among Eagles fans and media, but a Steelers offensive line that just lost Mason McCormick should still be plenty concerned about his presence. Even in a “down” year, Carter’s five sacks are only two off the NFL lead for defensive tackles. Jalen Carter made his presence felt all game against Jacksonville. 5 TKL, 3 TFL, 2 SACK, 2 FF, 1 PD vs Jaguars Even in the loss, Carter was one of Philly’s biggest difference makers on defense. pic.twitter.com/NkV1yK8k0C — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) October 11, 2026 As a defense, the Eagles’ 16 sacks on the season rank 28th, and their 109 pressures rank 26th. According to Next Gen Stats, the Eagles are below league average in blitz rate (26% vs 32%), and in generating pressure, whether that’s with the blitz (41% vs 43%) or without (30% vs 33%). Carter’s 20 pressures this season are tied for second on the Eagles behind only Moro Ojomo (22), an upcoming defensive tackle who allowed the Eagles the flexibility to trade away Davis. Jalyx Hunt, a rotational pass rusher who hasn’t played more than 43% of the defensive snaps in a game since Week 4, is tied with Carter. Nolan Smith (17 pressures, 5 sacks), Jonathan Greenard (11 pressures, 1 sack), and Zack Baun (9 pressures, 2 sacks) round out the Eagles’ underperforming pass rush. Baun, the Eagles’ top off-ball linebacker, is out for the game, the team announced Friday. With the lack of pressure, the Eagles’ secondary has predictably struggled. Third-year nickel corner Cooper DeJean has taken a step back, allowing four touchdowns this season after allowing just one during his first two seasons, and he has nearly as many missed tackles this season (13) as he had in his career (19) before this season. Meanwhile, Riq Woolen remains a volatile corner who has looked like a shutdown player some weeks and like a weak link in others, including surrendering four touchdowns against zero interceptions so far this season. If there is one bright spot in Philadelphia’s secondary, it’s cornerback Quinyon Mitchell, who is still performing at a high level. He’s allowed just a 55.6% catch rate and a QB passer rating of 76.5 when targeted. Philadelphia has typically let Mitchell stick to one side of the field, but in their most recent game, the Eagles finally tasked Mitchell with shadowing an opponent’s number one receiver. Against the Giants, Mitchell followed Malik Nabers and shut down New York’s most explosive playmaker. Quinyon Mitchell traveling with Malik Nabers today: – 3 targets – 2 catches allowed – 7 yards – 0 1st downs – 0 TDs – 1 PBU Death, taxes & #27 is gonna play like an All Pro. pic.twitter.com/ryqi6utrHj — garrett (@jalenreagors) November 8, 2026 As for what coverages we can expect from Philadelphia, the Eagles are a team that has lived in both nickel (68% of defensive snaps) packages and single-high safety looks (54% of snaps) for multiple seasons now. That has most typically shown up as Cover-3 looks in zone coverages (36.5%) and Cover-1 in man looks (15.3%). Defensive coverages weeks 1-10 via @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/kHyr8wIvIn — Football Insights 📊 (@fball_insights) November 17, 2026 On the ground, the Eagles aren’t quite as bad as the numbers might indicate. While the Eagles’ raw run defense totals look poor, they’re mostly in the middle of the pack in most metrics, and are surrendering a high yardage per game total mostly because they have been in negative game scripts for much of the season. Philadelphia allows the seventh-fewest average yards before contact (0.81); however, they also allow the eighth-highest average yards after contact (3.33). As a unit, they’ve missed 43 tackles on running plays, per PFF, but only DeJean (8) and safety Andrew Mukuba (6) are particularly heinous in this regard. No other defender has more than three missed tackles against the run. Philadelphia ranks 15th in stuffed run percentage (17%), but are tied with the Vikings and Patriots for the 13th-most runs of 10+ yards allowed (27). In theory, the Steelers’ strength — running the ball — should fare respectably against this Eagles front. However, the loss of Mason McCormick cannot be overstated. Spencer Anderson takes his spot and has shown a troubling deficiency in play strength and power thus far in his career. He’s excelled on the edges as a sixth offensive lineman, where he can take on lighter and less powerful defenders. Having him line up against Carter, though, gives me pause. Meanwhile, the Eagles’ secondary should be gettable, but Rodgers has not played well this season. The Eagles haven’t gotten pressure consistently, but Rodgers has often found his way into pressure even when the line is holding well. Now, without McCormick, there is potentially an easier path for the Philadelphia defensive line to get into the face of Pittsburgh’s mobility-challenged passer. This could be another frustrating day for the Black and Gold offense.

stories.title: Pat Freiermuth says Steelers still believe in DK Metcalf
stories.summary: Steelers TE Pat Freiermuth says team still believes in DK Metcalf.
stories.detailText: (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images DK Metcalf hasn’t quite lived up to expectations during his time in Pittsburgh, but that hasn’t shaken the confidence of his teammates. Pat Freiermuth opened up to the media today about the embattled wideout’s time in the Steel City. “Obviously he’s had some struggles but if you look at his effort on the run game or downfield blocking, he doesn’t let his situation impact his ability to get other guys open,” said Freiermuth on Thursday afternoon. “I think that’s something that you can appreciate as a teammate and as a guy you can tell a lot about his character. You know, we’re with him until the end. He’s going to get this figured out. We’ve got a lot of trust in DK and a lot of belief in him. We paid him for a reason, and the Steelers have backed him for a reason.” #Steelers believe in DK Metcalf. Pat Freiermuth explains pic.twitter.com/r65haJHhGC — 93.7 The Fan (@937theFan) November 19, 2026 Metcalf’s struggles have been a combination of costly drops, difficulty creating separation against physical coverage and inconsistency in the Steelers’ passing game. Opposing defenses have increasingly focused on limiting his opportunities, while Pittsburgh has leaned heavily on its running game. The Steelers acquired Metcalf to be their No. 1 receiving threat, and his physical tools and big-play ability remain undeniable. He previously established himself as one of the NFL’s more productive receivers in Seattle, recording 6,324 receiving yards and 48 touchdowns from 2019-2024. While the production hasn’t consistently followed him to Pittsburgh, Freiermuth’s confidence suggests the locker room still believes Metcalf can turn things around. The challenge now is translating his talent into more consistent results on the field. Let us know what you think in the comments . stories.title: Sources: Tom Brady buys stake in Chelsea after Birmingham exit
stories.summary: Seven-time Super Bowl champion quarterback Tom Brady has invested in Chelsea soccer club, sources confirmed to ESPN and NFL Network.
stories.detailText: Seven-time Super Bowl champion quarterback Tom Brady has purchased a stake in Chelsea soccer club, sources confirmed to ESPN and NFL Network. The deal would make the NFL legend a minority investor in the Clearlake Capital vehicle that controls Chelsea, sources close to global investment firm added to ESPN. Brady is expected to serve as an operating adviser to Clearlake but would not have voting rights with the club. Brady left the ownership group of second-tier English club Birmingham City earlier this month after becoming a minority owner with a 3.3% stake. Defense attorney Alex Spiro is part of Brady's ownership group and helped negotiate the deal. Brady had also held a position on the club's advisory board via a partnership with Birmingham's owner, Knighthead Capital Management, headed by his friend and business partner Tom Wagner. Todd Boehly and fellow co-owner Mark Walter sold their stakes in Chelsea this past September in a deal that gives Clearlake Capital full control of the English Premier League club. Private equity firm Clearlake, led by Behdad Eghbali and Jose E. Feliciano, previously owned a 61.5% stake in Chelsea, while U.S. businessmen Walter and Boehly each owned 12.83%. Swiss philanthropist Hansjörg Wyss, who also owned a 12.83% stake, remains a partner in the ownership group. The consortium bought Chelsea for £2.5 billion ($3.3 billion) in 2022 with a further £1.75 billion ($2.3 billion) committed to investment in the club after former owner Roman Abramovich was sanctioned because of alleged ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin following the country's invasion of Ukraine. The Financial Times reported that Walter and Boehly will receive £950 million ($1.3 billion) for their combined stake in a deal that values the club at £5 billion ($6.7 billion) including debt. Neither Chelsea nor Clearlake Capital has replied to ESPN's request for comment about Brady's purchase of shares. Brady purchased a 5% minority stake in the Las Vegas Raiders in 2024 after NFL owners unanimously approved the deal. ESPN's Adam Schefter and James Olley as well as NFL Network's Ian Rapoport contributed to this report.

stories.title: Where the 49ers need to improve defensively vs. Vikings
stories.summary: What were the Niners main issues defensively against the Cowboys?
stories.detailText: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 15: Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers rushes the passer during a game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last weekend was not a good day for the San Francisco 49ers defense, as they gave up 40 points on the Dallas Cowboys, yet still managed to come away with the 46-40 victory. San Francisco’s defense struggled on all fronts. The secondary especially had its issues, as Dallas’s top three receivers all had quality games. George Pickens had 11 catches for 145 yards and three touchdowns, and that was with him dropping three passes. CeeDee Lamb had seven catches for 72 yards and a touchdown, while Ryan Flournoy had six catches for 71 yards and a touchdown. Cornerbacks Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green, and Upton Stout entered the game banged up, and it showed, as both had their fair share of struggles against Dallas’s elite offense. Of course, the matchup wasn’t easy facing a high-caliber quarterback with two Pro Bowl receivers, but it was a rough day for a defense that had been quite good over the first half of the season. That wasn’t the only issue. The 49ers pass rush was also ineffective, failing to sack Dak Prescott, and Nick Bosa came out this week and took accountability for his play this season. Bosa has yet to record a sack, although his other numbers still indicate a productive season, especially with the double teams and chips he’s facing. Now, this week, the health is looking better. Stout remained limited in practice with his ongoing shoulder injury and is questionable, but Lenoir wasn’t on the injury report and Renardo Green practiced in full on Thursday and is off the injury report for Sunday’s game. But the 49ers still have a tough challenge against the Minnesota Vikings, who put up 30 points on the Green Bay Packers in Kirk Cousins’s return. Minnesota’s offense suddenly looks formidable, and this battle should be a tough one on both sides. After their struggles against Dallas, where do the 49ers need to improve defensively against Minnesota? Ahead of Sunday night, defensive coordinator Raheem Morris broke down the main issues he saw from the Cowboys game and what to take from it. “Extending drives early with some of the penalties to get those guys to go down there, particularly on the first drive [was a problem]. We gave up three, I believe, on that first one,” Morris said. “We got the big penalty to get those guys down there. They got a big-time field goal kicker. A couple of big plays in the first half. The two big plays were the ones that killed us there early. Got a pretty good grip on it after that and kind of held it down. It was at some point it was like 38-19. Then that finishing moments, we didn’t do a very good job of getting the finishes off. Usually, the finishes happen when you’re able to generate pressure with sacks or you’re able to get interceptions. “The Cowboys did a nice job, to give them credit, of getting the ball out of their hand. Did a nice job of getting the ball into their good players’ hand, keeping drives going, extending drives. They had about three or four drives there where it was almost like overtime-like play for them, where it was going to be fourth down territory regardless and they were able to capitalize and go down and score on us. You would like to be able to stop some of those plays and be able to get those guys going and get off the grass at those moments and then that score wouldn’t have got to where it was, but those things didn’t happen. “We didn’t execute that way. And it’s a collective group. I know [Nick] Bosa stood up in front of you guys and took all the credit and took all the accountability, but I really think it’s just all of us. Some of it could be better play calls for them. Some of it could be better for us, what we can do for those guys. Some of it can be better plays made by us. Some of it, we just ran out a little bit of gas, got a little bit tired. Let’s not kid ourselves. Human nature as well. So, fortunate to get out of there with a win. Definitely want to learn those lessons when you get a chance to do those things in those moments, when you get wins. Something that we can learn from and grow from and something that we definitely will.” One thing Morris did see from his team was accountability after the game, with the leaders on the team stepping up. “They’re such an accountable group,” Morris added. “Most guys, you come in and you’re just upset after a game. These guys, they hold themselves to such a high standard. They come in, they’re able to speak very clearly right off the bat. So it’s not going to be more vocal the next week because they were vocal the first week. Not necessarily Bosa. Bosa’s kind of a to-himself guy, but for a guy like Fred [Warner], he’s always going to speak up and do the things that happened. It wasn’t like there was mistakes. They did some better job executing. There was a few mistakes. There’s always going to be mistakes and there’s always correcting mistakes. I’m not saying there’s not mistakes, but there’s always going to be correcting mistakes, but you correct those mistakes, you move on. “There’s some other things that, just you talking to as an individual player. The best thing about our guys, they always point at themselves first. Whether it’s Fred, whether it’s Bosa, whether it’s DMo (Deommodore Lenoir), Renardo [Green], anybody on our football team. That’s the cool part about being here with these guys is they point at themselves first. Then a lot of the times I’m able to say, ‘Hey, I can help you here’ or ‘we can do these things better. We can make these calls. We can help you out, do a little bit better in these situations.’ They are all so upfront and forthgoing with those things. That makes it really cool to talk to those guys that way.” Health seemed to be a factor last weekend, but the 49ers do need to be more disciplined and avoid the killer penalties (although some looked to be questionable calls). But there is a lot at stake this weekend for the 49ers, as their No. 1 seed odds shift dramatically with a win or a loss. San Francisco’s offense has always been up to the task, but they’ll get their toughest matchup of the year with Brian Flores’s defense. So, the 49ers defense will need to show up as well against this new-look Vikings offense with Kirk Cousins and execute on all three levels.
